title: Failure statistical characteristics of material after technological deformation treatment
source: Journal of Applied Mathematics and Computational Mechanics
summary: This paper presents an algorithm to calculate the statistical strength characteristics of stochastically defective plate elements of structures in a plane stress field, accounting for the directional structure of defects resulting from a sp
content: This paper presents an algorithm to calculate the statistical strength characteristics of stochastically defective plate elements of structures in a plane stress field, accounting for the directional structure of defects resulting from a specific technological deformation treatment.Defects such as cracks weaken structural elements and do not interact with each other; they are characterized by two statistically independent parameters: length and orientation angle.Based on analytical representations of the integral probability distribution function of failure loading, a relationship was obtained to determine the mean value and dispersion of strength.Diagrams of changes in statistical strength characteristics for plates of different scales and types of loading and treatment coefficients were constructed.

title: Optimization and integration of solar PV systems for sustainable energy transition in Indonesia
source: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
summary: Indonesia’s growing demand for clean and reliable electricity requires effective renewable energy integration. Solar photovoltaic (PV) technology offers substantial potential due to the country’s abundant solar resources, although variation
content: Indonesia’s growing demand for clean and reliable electricity requires effective renewable energy integration. Solar photovoltaic (PV) technology offers substantial potential due to the country’s abundant solar resources, although variations in solar irradiance, system performance, and investment costs remain significant challenges. This study aims to optimize and evaluate solar PV integration based on technical performance and economic feasibility to support Indonesia’s sustainable energy transition. A quantitative approach is applied to analyze solar irradiance, PV energy production, system efficiency, capacity factor, investment and operational costs, levelized cost of energy (LCOE), and net present cost (NPC). Various system configurations and operating scenarios are assessed to identify the most effective combination of PV capacity and components. The results are expected to determine an optimal configuration that ensures reliable energy production, improved technical performance, and competitive energy costs. Furthermore, the study examines the relationship between technical performance and economic indicators to support researchers, policymakers, and energy planners in developing sustainable and economically viable solar PV systems in Indonesia.

title: Sustainable Design of Lightweight Low-Clinker Mortars Incorporating Recycled Ceramic Constituents
summary: The development of lightweight low-clinker cementitious materials requires simultaneous optimization of mechanical performance, density, workability, and sustainability.This study investigates the combined effects of ceramic brick powder, s
content: The development of lightweight low-clinker cementitious materials requires simultaneous optimization of mechanical performance, density, workability, and sustainability.This study investigates the combined effects of ceramic brick powder, sodium sulphate, and cellulose ether on lightweight slag-cement mortars incorporating recycled ceramic fine aggregate. A D-optimal experimental design coupled with response surface methodology was employed to develop predictive experimental-statistical models. Fresh-state performance was evaluated through the superplasticizer demand required to maintain a constant flow spread of 140-150 mm, while hardened properties included density, compressive strength, flexural strength, and structural efficiency. The developed models were validated experimentally, yielding prediction errors below 3%. The investigated mortars achieved 28-day dry densities of 1790-1850 kg/m³, compressive strengths of 52-58 MPa, and flexural strengths of 7.6-8.8 MPa.Response surface analysis demonstrated that the engineering performance was governed by the combined interaction of varied composition factors. A constraint-based optimization identified an optimum mixture incorporating approximately 249 kg/m³ of ceramic brick powder while satisfying the target requirements for compressive strength (≥55 MPa), flexural strength (≥8 MPa), and dry density (≤1820 kg/m³). Compared with the reference mixture, the optimized composition reduced cement consumption by approximately 32%, corresponding to estimated reductions of about 119 kg CO₂-eq./m³ and 0.69 GJ/m³ of embodied energy. The proposed methodology provides an effective framework for designing resource-efficient lightweight structural mortars containing recycled ceramic constituents.

title: Rice Husk Ash as a Partial Replacement of Cement in Concrete
source: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
summary: Rice husk ash (RHA) is a silica-rich residue obtained from the combustion of rice husks. Its potential use as a supplementary cementitious material is of interest because Portland cement manufacture is carbon intensive and rice milling gene
content: Rice husk ash (RHA) is a silica-rich residue obtained from the combustion of rice husks. Its potential use as a supplementary cementitious material is of interest because Portland cement manufacture is carbon intensive and rice milling generates substantial agricultural residues. This paper critically reviews the mechanisms by which properly processed RHA affects concrete, identifies factors controlling performance, and proposes a laboratory program to compare ordinary concrete with mixtures incorporating 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% RHA as a mass replacement for cement. The review considers ash production, amorphous silica, particle fineness, water demand, fresh properties, compressive and tensile strength, and durability. Existing studies support the feasibility of moderate cement replacement, but no single replacement percentage can be claimed optimal for all sources and mixture designs. A controlled experimental protocol and transparent results-reporting framework are developed for undergraduate research. Keywords Rice husk ash; supplementary cementitious material; pozzolanic reaction; sustainable concrete; compressive strength; workability; durability. Research questions How does replacement of cement with locally produced RHA affect workability and mechanical performance? Which processing and mix-design factors most strongly influence the result? Can the use of RHA reduce cement demand without compromising specified performance?

title: Green Marketing in the Insurance Industry: An ESG Analysis of Selected Indian Insurance Companies
source: Saudi Journal of Business and Management Studies
summary: Financial-service companies, including insurance companies, are increasingly taking environmental sustainability into account. Insurers are increasingly encountering climate-related risks and are expected to address the concerns of stakehol
content: Financial-service companies, including insurance companies, are increasingly taking environmental sustainability into account. Insurers are increasingly encountering climate-related risks and are expected to address the concerns of stakeholders, which has led to ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) being incorporated into insurers' strategy and corporate communications. This research explores the green marketing practices of the selected insurance companies in India from the year 2021 up to February 2025. A multiple case method, qualitative approach was employed based on public information in the company disclosures, press releases and industry sources. The study is based on the case studies of four insurance companies: Axis Max Life Insurance, PNB MetLife, Generali Central Insurance, and Future Generali India Insurance. The analysis reveals three key patterns: community-based afforestation, a culture of employee engagement with sustainable practices, as well as embedding environmental initiatives in corporate brand communication. Over 7000 saplings were planted in 35 cities with more than 1700 volunteers under Axis Max Life's Insure Earth program and PNB MetLife's Glow Green program, aimed at planting and nurturing more than 40000 trees. Future General, Generali's Green Switch program gamified the way their employees behaved to make them more environmentally friendly. The results indicate that green marketing in the insurance sector is not just about communicating CSR, but also about engaging more with stakeholders and promoting the sustainability of the organization. But company-reported environmental outcomes must be interpreted with caution, as they are not necessarily a reflection of independent verification of ESG performance. Thus, the key to successful green marketing is transparency, measurable indicators and credible environmental claims.

title: Gastric metastasis from renal cell carcinoma with a 10-year interval: A case report
summary: BACKGROUND Gastric metastasis of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is rare clinically, often presenting with a prolonged interval (median 7-10 years) between initial diagnosis and metastasis, rendering it prone to imaging oversight. CASE SUMMARY W
content: BACKGROUND Gastric metastasis of renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is rare clinically, often presenting with a prolonged interval (median 7-10 years) between initial diagnosis and metastasis, rendering it prone to imaging oversight. CASE SUMMARY We report a 70-year-old man with advanced clear cell RCC (ccRCC) who developed gastric metastasis 10 years after initial radical nephrectomy. After adjuvant therapy with interleukin-2 and treatment of subsequent recurrent left renal pelvis RCC with partial nephrectomy and pazopanib, the patient received penpulimab plus axitinib for metastatic disease. A gastric fundus mass was detected by positron emission tomography/computed tomography during routine follow-up and confirmed as metastatic ccRCC by endoscopic biopsy and immunohistochemistry (PAX-8+, CA IX+, CD10+, CK7-). The patient underwent robot-assisted wedge resection of the stomach in August 2025 and remains on sintilimab maintenance immunotherapy. CONCLUSION For advanced RCC, gastric metastasis should remain part of differential diagnosis even in the absence of gastrointestinal symptoms.

title: S³: A Multicriteria Pre-Deployment Scoring Protocol for Enterprise Small Language Model Selection
source: Journal of Artificial Intelligence & Cloud Computing
summary: Technology managers lack a systematic protocol for determining which enterprise workloads are safe for local small language model deployment. We introduce S³ (Suitability Score for SLM Selection), a multicriteria framework that scores workl
content: Technology managers lack a systematic protocol for determining which enterprise workloads are safe for local small language model deployment. We introduce S³ (Suitability Score for SLM Selection), a multicriteria framework that scores workloads across six dimensions, Task Complexity, Output Structure, Stakeholder Risk, Data Sensitivity, Latency Tolerance, and Volume Load, and assigns them to Pure SLM, Hybrid, or LLM-Only tiers before inference. Non-compensatory gate rules enforce safety constraints for high-stakes scenarios, ensuring that life-critical or expert-level generative tasks are never assigned to a local model regardless of their aggregate score. Thresholds calibrated on an independent use-case set correctly predicted all eight held-out tier assignments across six industries, with Pure SLM tiers achieving at least 95% LLM parity.

title: JWST detects a dusty AGB-like source before the Type Ia-CSM supernova 2026sqf
summary: Supernova (SN) 2026sqf recently appeared in the nearby face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3310 and has shown signs of strong interaction with a circumstellar medium (CSM). Such an intense interaction, rare among nearby SNe, offers a valuable opportu
content: Supernova (SN) 2026sqf recently appeared in the nearby face-on spiral galaxy NGC 3310 and has shown signs of strong interaction with a circumstellar medium (CSM). Such an intense interaction, rare among nearby SNe, offers a valuable opportunity to reveal details of the origin and nature of its progenitor system. We present early-time photometric and spectroscopic observations of SN 2026sqf, along with our identification and characterization of a candidate pre-explosion counterpart in space telescope imaging. We analyzed the early-phase spectra and light curves (LCs) of SN 2026sqf. We identified a point source near the SN position in pre-explosion JWST and HST imaging, tested its association with the SN through astrometric alignment of pre- and post-explosion images and a chance-projection analysis, and constructed and modeled its spectral energy distribution (SED). The general characteristics of the spectra, the strengths of the emission lines, and the LC evolution all suggest that SN 2026sqf belongs to the rare SN Ia-CSM subclass, which would make it the closest known member (D ∼ 19 Mpc). The point source is a credible counterpart of the progenitor system, the first such identification for this SN subclass. Under our modeling assumptions, carbonaceous dust around a luminous evolved star provides a reasonable description of its combined SED; compared with local analogues, the candidate most closely resembles an extreme asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star. We report the first candidate pre-explosion counterpart of a thermonuclear SN identified in JWST imaging. Our results support the scenario in which SNe Ia-CSM emerge from a system consisting of a white dwarf and an evolved giant (probably AGB) star. Strong binary interaction, possibly involving common-envelope evolution or a merger, is a natural explanation for the observed properties of the SN and its candidate counterpart, although the channel and timescale remain uncertain. Late-time follow-up, especially with JWST, will allow us to test the identification and the conclusions of our early-phase analysis.

title: Vegan Intersections: Histories, Literature, Texts
summary: The contributions gathered in this collection advance the growing field of Critical Vegan Studies, and specifically Vegan Cultural Studies, by exploring a developing corpus of “vegan” texts in film, literature, and other discursive forms. C
content: The contributions gathered in this collection advance the growing field of Critical Vegan Studies, and specifically Vegan Cultural Studies, by exploring a developing corpus of “vegan” texts in film, literature, and other discursive forms. Contributors test emergent concepts of vegan cultural production and vegan analytical methodologies that can be applied both to texts that are intentionally “vegan” and to those that may pre-date or situate themselves outside the practice of veganism. The interventions collected here pursue these aims most intensely in the context of literature and film, media that explore imaginatively and speculatively the tensions between the liberationist values of vegan idealism or utopianism, and the reality of anthropocentrism and speciesism that undergird the mainstream ideology of carnism. Contributors focus primarily on Anglo-American texts and contexts, highlighting vegan intersections among a diversity of social justice issues spanning the period from the early nineteenth century to the present.

title: Shock-driven evolution of a hydrogenated amorphous carbon analog: Pathways to small hydrocarbons, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and fullerenes
summary: Hydrogenated amorphous carbon (HAC) is ubiquitous in the interstellar medium (ISM). However, the contribution of shock-processed HAC to the formation of large carbonaceous molecules, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and ful
content: Hydrogenated amorphous carbon (HAC) is ubiquitous in the interstellar medium (ISM). However, the contribution of shock-processed HAC to the formation of large carbonaceous molecules, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and fullerenes, remains largely unexplored. In this work, we examined the chemical products and transformations associated with shock processing of HAC particles by investigating the gaseous volatiles and solid residues . We used polystyrene (PS) as a proxy for HAC. produced We a pressure-driven shock tube to heat PS particles to employed ∼ 4000,K. We monitored the time-dependent shock processing of PS in situ using optical emission spectroscopy. We further analyzed the gaseous products with the help of gas chromatography. We collected the solid residues and analyzed them ex situ using a variety of methods including infrared microspectroscopy, Raman microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and laser desorption ionization mass spectrometry. molecular dynamics and chemical kinetic modeling, the experimental findings. We performed simulations which support Shock processing induces rapid heating, during which extensive dehydrogenation and fragmentation of PS occur, accompanied by the release of H_2 and small hydrocarbons. From this hot chemistry, a diversity of large molecular species, including PAHs, emerges. An H-poor solid material that contains graphitic structures is produced during cooling. The shock-induced thermal processing of HAC involves both top-down and bottom-up mechanisms that generate small hydrocarbons, PAHs, and fullerenes. The rapid destruction of HAC-like material, followed by molecular reassembly, offers a plausible explanation for the coexistence of abundant small hydrocarbons and a variety of carbonaceous dust species, including PAHs , in the ISM.

title: Normalizing sustainable fashion innovations: environmental messages and dynamic norms in circular fashion adoption
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether informational messages promote interest in fashion products made from agri-food waste and whether dynamic norm cues strengthen persuasion in a trend-sensitive, ambiguous market. Design/methodol
content: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether informational messages promote interest in fashion products made from agri-food waste and whether dynamic norm cues strengthen persuasion in a trend-sensitive, ambiguous market. Design/methodology/approach Overall, 183 Italian adults were randomly assigned to control, environmental message or environmental plus dynamic norm message conditions. Participants reported purchasing intention and willingness to pay a premium price. Pro-environmental self-identity and identification with sustainable fashion consumers were tested as moderators. Findings Only the combined environmental and dynamic norm message increased purchasing intention, whereas neither message affected willingness to pay, suggesting a distinction between motivational interest and financial commitment. Exploratory analyses suggested that the environmental message was more effective among participants with low identification with sustainable fashion consumers. Pro-environmental self-identity did not moderate message effects. Research limitations/implications Self-reported intentions and a highly educated Italian sample limit generalisability. Future studies should use behavioural measures, field experiments, longitudinal designs and diverse samples to test whether initial openness persists and translates into purchasing and price acceptance. Practical implications Environmental messages combined with dynamic norm cues can increase initial interest in agri-food waste fashion, but the promotional strategy did not increase willingness to pay, highlighting the importance of product, price and audience segmentation. Originality/value The study shows that integrating dynamic norm cues into environmental appeals can increase initial openness toward novel sustainable fashion products, while purchasing intention and willingness to pay represent distinct outcomes for intervention design.

title: Knowledge and competency framework for quantity surveyors to perform circular economy practices successfully in the construction industry
summary: Purpose The construction industry significantly contributes to resource depletion and waste generation, necessitating the adoption of circular economy (CE) practices. The successful implementation of CE practices depends on the knowledge an
content: Purpose The construction industry significantly contributes to resource depletion and waste generation, necessitating the adoption of circular economy (CE) practices. The successful implementation of CE practices depends on the knowledge and competencies of construction professionals, particularly quantity surveyors (QSs), whose cost, procurement and contractual decisions strongly influence CE adoption. Therefore, this study aims to develop a knowledge and competency framework for QSs to perform CE practices successfully in the construction industry. Design/methodology/approach An interpretive research philosophy with a qualitative approach was adopted using the Delphi technique. A two-round Delphi study was conducted involving 20 experts in Round 1 and 17 experts in Round 2, resulting in a total of 37 interviews. The data were analysed through code-based content analysis using NVivo14. Findings The findings highlight QS involvement across design, construction and end-of-life stages, identifying 14 significant CE practices. The study further identifies 17 common knowledge areas and 60 competencies, along with 11 QS-specific knowledge areas and 21 competencies required for each CE practice. Originality/value This study contributes to academic discourse by developing and empirically validating a comprehensive framework encompassing QS-specific knowledge areas, QS-specific competencies, common competencies and common knowledge areas. The core contribution of this study is in identifying QS-specific knowledge areas and competencies and systematically mapping them to the specific CE practices that QSs can perform across the project life cycle. For industry professionals, the framework assists in identifying, assessing and enhancing the specific knowledge areas and competencies required to effectively engage with CE practices to successfully embed CE into the construction industry.

title: Understanding Energy Consumption in Autonomous Vehicles: A Component-Level Analysis
summary: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are becoming an increasingly visible part of the transportation landscape, with various models and companies deploying fleets across different regions. The impact of AVs has been examined in the literature in terms
content: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are becoming an increasingly visible part of the transportation landscape, with various models and companies deploying fleets across different regions. The impact of AVs has been examined in the literature in terms of driving style, speed, and travel demand effects. However, research on their operational energy consumption remains limited. AV components vary by manufacturer, such as in the number of sensors, redundancy strategies, and the efficiency of computing platforms, which directly affect energy consumption and emissions per kilometer. In this study, we analyzed how different component configurations influence the energy consumption of AVs on the road. Our results show that AV sensors and onboard computers contribute to power demand through their own auxiliary power demand and by increasing the drag coefficient and vehicle mass. We also find that the dominant sources of additional power consumption vary substantially with vehicle speed.

title: Toward a Digital Twin Framework for Urban Mobility Innovation - A Versailles Grand Parc Case Study
summary: Urban mobility faces simultaneous challenges of decarbonization and air quality improvement, requiring adaptive tools for planning and policy evaluation. This paper presents a digital twin (DT) framework that integrates agent-based modeling
content: Urban mobility faces simultaneous challenges of decarbonization and air quality improvement, requiring adaptive tools for planning and policy evaluation. This paper presents a digital twin (DT) framework that integrates agent-based modeling of personal and freight mobility with automatic calibration using real-time sensor and GPS data. Structured around three components—modeling daily mobility dynamics, continuous calibration, and decision-support applications—the DT captures multimodal flows, temporal variations, and emissions at street-level resolution. Applied to Versailles Grand Parc, the framework generates actionable outputs for diverse stakeholders: informative indicators for the public, detailed traffic and emission maps for city services, and predictive analyses for policy evaluation, including Low Emission Zones. By combining high-resolution simulation with adaptive data-driven calibration, the DT provides a robust, integrated tool to support sustainable urban mobility and environmental decision-making.

title: MMVNet - Designing the Data Future of Multi-modal Transport in Germany
summary: Transport and traffic planning in Germany are predominantly organized along single-mode lines, with road, rail, and inland waterway systems treated in isolation. A key barrier to integrated planning is the absence of an up-to-date, consiste
content: Transport and traffic planning in Germany are predominantly organized along single-mode lines, with road, rail, and inland waterway systems treated in isolation. A key barrier to integrated planning is the absence of an up-to-date, consistent, routable and referenceable dataset spanning all three major transport modalities. To address this issue, we present the multi-modal transport network data model MMVNet that integrates Germany’s fragmented transport infrastructure data into a unified, publicly-available dataset. This approach addresses technical challenges including heterogeneous data models, inconsistent referencing systems, and coverage gaps by establishing a service architecture built upon established standards. Quality assurance methods, including validation via remote sensing imagery, maintain data accuracy across all modes. The resulting dataset represents a federally-owned, comprehensive multi-modal transport network for Germany, supporting public sector planning and private sector innovation while advancing digital sovereignty goals.

title: Diet composition, staple-food dependence and structural patterns of dietary diversity: a global analysis using FAOSTAT food balance sheet data
summary: Dietary diversity is a key indicator of nutritional adequacy and a crucial component of sustainable food systems. Nonetheless, the roles of plant- and animal-derived foods in shaping dietary diversity outcomes at national and global levels
content: Dietary diversity is a key indicator of nutritional adequacy and a crucial component of sustainable food systems. Nonetheless, the roles of plant- and animal-derived foods in shaping dietary diversity outcomes at national and global levels are still not fully understood. Using the FAOSTAT dataset and the Simpson diversity index, this study examines the association between plant-derived food-energy share and national dietary diversity. We use 2015–2017 FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheet (FBS) data covering 182 countries. Country-level dietary diversity was calculated using the Simpson index, and its association with the plant-derived share of food energy was assessed using Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Plant-derived food-energy share was significantly negatively associated with Simpson diversity ( r = − 0.485, p < 0.01). Several countries in sub-Saharan Africa combined a high plant-derived energy share of 90% with Simpson scores of 0.90. Nevertheless, their national food-energy supplies were often concentrated in a small number of leading foods, with the five largest contributors accounting for 65–75% of available energy. By contrast, European and North American nations achieved similarly high Simpson scores of 0.90–0.95 through a less concentrated distribution of energy across cereals, animal-derived foods, oils, sweeteners and other food groups. These contrasting patterns reveal a structural dietary diversity paradox in which similar numerical scores represent conceptually different situations. We describe a high score that coexists with marked staple-food concentration as absolute diversity , whereas qualitative diversity denotes a high numerical score accompanied by broader and more balanced food-group composition. The findings demonstrate that diet diversity should be interpreted alongside staple concentration and food-group composition. This approach could consequently support more cautious nutrition-security monitoring and more context-sensitive policies relating to Sustainable Development Goal 2.

title: CrSe2 and CrTe2 Monolayers as Efficient Nanosensors for Air Pollutants
summary: Nanosensors are critical in environmental monitoring, industrial safety, and public health by detecting specific hazardous gases such as CO, NO, SO2, and CH4 at trace levels. This study uses density functional theory (DFT) calculations to e
content: Nanosensors are critical in environmental monitoring, industrial safety, and public health by detecting specific hazardous gases such as CO, NO, SO2, and CH4 at trace levels. This study uses density functional theory (DFT) calculations to examine the gas-sensing capabilities of chromium diselenide (CrSe2) and chromium ditelluride (CrTe2) monolayers through their structural and electronic responses to gas adsorption. Adsorption energy (Eads) analysis shows that Te vacancy-induced CrTe2 (VTe-CrTe2) exhibits the strongest binding with energies of −1.52, −1.79, and −1.61 eV for CO, NO, and SO2, respectively. Similarly, pristine CrSe2 exhibits moderate Eads values of −1.13, −1.17, −0.90, and −1.12 eV for CO, NO, SO2, and CH4, respectively; while room-temperature recovery remains prolonged for CO, NO, and CH4(τ ∼ 106–107s), practical sensor reversibility is readily achievable under mild thermal activation (up to 400 K). This study also investigates how substitutional doping of Ge, Sb, and Sn influences the sensing mechanism of CrSe2 and CrTe2 monolayers. Density of states (DOS) analysis highlights notable electronic changes around the Fermi level, especially in VTe-CrTe2 and Sb/Sn-doped CrTe2, confirming their enhanced sensing abilities. Charge density difference analysis shows significant charge redistribution, with CrTe2 experiencing stronger charge transfer effects than CrSe2. Variations in electrostatic potential and work function further demonstrate the higher sensitivity of CrTe2, particularly in its defective and doped forms, confirming its status as a superior material for gas-sensing applications.

title: Earthworm functional traits drive greenhouse gas emissions from casts through their effects on microbial and physicochemical properties
summary: Earthworms strongly influence soil biogeochemical processes, and their casts can act as microsites of GHG production. However, the main biotic and abiotic determinants driving GHG emissions from earthworm casts and their links to earthworm
content: Earthworms strongly influence soil biogeochemical processes, and their casts can act as microsites of GHG production. However, the main biotic and abiotic determinants driving GHG emissions from earthworm casts and their links to earthworm functional traits remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of nine earthworm species across two contrasting soil types on CO 2 and N 2 O emissions and potential CH 4 production from casts produced under controlled conditions. We hypothesized that these GHG responses are determined by specific earthworm traits influencing cast physicochemical properties and the abundance of microbial functional groups. To this end, we measured 21 morpho-anatomical, physiological, and behavioral traits for each earthworm species and quantified CO 2 and N 2 O emissions, potential CH 4 production, cast properties, and microbial functional gene abundances in casts produced in Cambisol and Luvisol soils. Compared with control soil aggregates from microcosms without earthworms, casts showed, on average, 8-fold higher CO 2 emissions, 7-fold higher N 2 O emissions, and 4-fold higher potential CH 4 production. Cast-specific GHG responses varied among species, with Lumbricus castaneus showing the highest CO 2 emissions (19-fold) and potential CH 4 production (11-fold), whereas Lumbricus terrestris showed the highest N 2 O emissions (22-fold). Scaling emissions by cast production rate and earthworm biomass altered species rankings, indicating that a species' potential GHG contribution depends on both cast-specific emission intensity and cast production per unit biomass. These species-specific patterns also depended on soil type. CO 2 and N 2 O emissions were strongly correlated with cast properties, including the abundances of total bacteria, ammonia oxidizers, and denitrifiers, as well as physicochemical parameters such as labile carbon pools (DOC and POM), mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM), nitrate availability, and moisture content. PLS-SEM analysis supported our hypothesis by revealing strong associations between earthworm traits, including litter ingestion, mouth area, gizzard mass, gut water content, and cast production, and CO 2 and N 2 O emissions through cast physicochemical and microbial properties, with significant indirect effects (β = 0.65and 0.78, respectively). These findings highlight a trait-based framework linking earthworm functional traits, casts properties, and GHG dynamics, and emphasize the need for field studies to assess how the combined influence of earthworm traits and soil conditions shapes fluxes under natural conditions.

title: Functionalized textile-based materials and textile waste-derived sorbents for carbon dioxide capture: current advances, performance evaluation, and future perspectives
summary: The textile industry is a significant contributor to global greenhouse-gas emissions, highlighting the need for both emission-reduction strategies and complementary carbon-management approaches. Beyond emission reduction strategies, textile
content: The textile industry is a significant contributor to global greenhouse-gas emissions, highlighting the need for both emission-reduction strategies and complementary carbon-management approaches. Beyond emission reduction strategies, textile materials offer an underexplored platform for carbon capture owing to their hierarchical porosity, flexibility, large surface area, and scalability. Although increasing research has explored modified textile substrates and textile waste-derived sorbents for CO 2 capture, these areas have largely developed independently. To the best of our knowledge, this review provides a comprehensive synthesis of both fields, establishing a unified perspective on textile resources for carbon capture and textile waste valorization. A PRISMA-guided literature selection process identified 27 core sources for detailed evaluation. Functionalized textile substrates incorporating porous carbons, metal–organic frameworks, amines, enzymes, and biological systems were assessed in terms of CO 2 capture mechanisms, adsorption performance, regeneration durability, and operating conditions. In parallel, textile waste conversion into CO 2 sorbents was examined from a circular economy perspective. Most reported gravimetric adsorption capacities at or near atmospheric pressure were below 5 mmol g⁻ 1 , although direct comparison was limited by differences in CO 2 partial pressure, temperature, humidity, and measurement method. The highest adsorption capacities were reported for viscose rayon-derived activated carbon cloth (14.30 mmol g⁻ 1 at 20 bar) and an amino acid ionic liquid-functionalized waste wool sorbent (11.75 mmol g −1 under pure CO 2 ). However, regeneration stability and long-term durability remain insufficiently investigated. Textile resources exhibit significant potential as sustainable CO 2 sorbents, while further research is needed to improve durability and practical implementation in circular carbon-management systems. Graphical Abstract Conceptual overview of textile-enabled CO 2 capture pathways. Textile materials can serve as functionalized capture platforms through activated carbon structures, amine modification, porous inorganic coatings, and biological systems, or they can be converted from textile waste into value-added CO 2 sorbents.

title: EIF5B /mitogen-activated protein kinase 1 axis drives tumor progression and confers dual resistance to chemotherapy and immunotherapy in colonic adenocarcinoma
summary: BACKGROUND Although eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5B (EIF5B ) is implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple malignancies, its functional impact in colonic adenocarcinoma (COAD) is still not well defined. AIM To determine EIF5B ’s
content: BACKGROUND Although eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5B (EIF5B ) is implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple malignancies, its functional impact in colonic adenocarcinoma (COAD) is still not well defined. AIM To determine EIF5B ’s role, mechanisms, and therapeutic associations in COAD. METHODS To assess the prognostic value of EIF5B , we integrated pan-cancer bioinformatic screening with clinical validation in COAD cohorts. The oncogenic function and molecular regulations were evaluated through in vitro and in vivo assays, multi-omic pathway enrichment, Western blotting, rescue experiments, immune infiltration and drug-sensitivity modeling. RESULTS Our results showed significant overexpression of EIF5B in COAD tissues, and its correlation with unfavorable patient outcomes. Functional analysis revealed that EIF5B induced migration, proliferation, and invasion in vitro , as well as promoted tumorigenesis in vivo through phosphorylation of mitogen-activated protein kinase 1 (MAPK1). In addition, the immune microenvironment exhibited a suppressed phenotype, accompanied by decreased predictive scores for programmed cell death protein 1/cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 blockade and reduced predicted sensitivity to chemotherapeutic agents. EIF5B expression, immune evasion, and drug sensitivity were associated with the MAPK signaling pathway. CONCLUSION EIF5B mediated phosphorylation of MAPK1 regulates the progression of COAD, suggesting EIF5B as potential therapeutic target for overcoming resistance against chemotherapy and immunotherapy.

title: Allocation and greenhouse gas accounting for CO2 utilisation: a steelworks-to-fuel case study
summary: Carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) can convert industrial CO 2 -rich gases into fuels and chemicals, but reported climate benefits depend strongly on system boundaries, allocation and carbon accounting choices. This study assesses a multi
content: Carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) can convert industrial CO 2 -rich gases into fuels and chemicals, but reported climate benefits depend strongly on system boundaries, allocation and carbon accounting choices. This study assesses a multifunctional steelworks-to-fuel system in which blast furnace gas is conditioned and converted with hydrogen to produce a propane-rich fuel. Two perspectives are evaluated: a gate-to-gate CCU plant perspective (functional unit: 1 kg CO 2 -based fuel, a propane/butane/ethane mix) and a cradle-to-gate steel plant perspective (1 kg hot rolled coil, HRC). Global Warming Potential (GWP) is compared across hydrogen sources, embedded-carbon treatment, life-cycle assessment (LCA)-based allocation and the Renewable Energy Directive III (RED III) method for recycled carbon fuels. From the CCU perspective, production-stage GWP ranged from 1.97 to 7.69 kg CO 2 eq./kg without an embedded-carbon credit, exceeding the fossil reference mixture of 1.15; the credit reduced this to −1.03 to 4.69, where negative values reflect accounting rather than permanent storage. From the steel perspective, the benefit of diverting blast furnace gas is small (6%) and can become unfavourable when fuel credits are balanced as burdens on steel. Mass allocation assigns 1.86 kg CO 2 eq./kg to the fuel, above the fossil reference, whereas economic allocation assigns 1.03 kg CO 2 eq./kg (0.91‐1.19 across observed annual prices), below it at mean prices; under system expansion, HRC instead receives avoided-production credits and no separate fuel footprint is calculated. Under RED III, including the use phase, the fuel reaches 99 g CO 2 eq./MJ, above the 94 g CO 2 eq./MJ fossil fuel comparator, because the credit for the carbon input is balanced by combustion emissions while gas conditioning and lost electricity generation are charged to the fuel. CCU fuels therefore require transparent treatment of CO 2 inputs, displaced products and accounting boundaries to avoid misleading claims and misaligned incentives between CO 2 source and user.

title: Evaluating a Low-Cost Forward Collision Warning System for Motorcycles: An Exploratory Naturalistic Riding Study in Urban Indonesia
summary: Motorcycle rider safety remains a critical issue, particularly in developing countries where two‑wheeled vehicles are disproportionately involved in crashes. This study evaluates the Motorcycle Collision‑Alert and Management System (MCAMS),
content: Motorcycle rider safety remains a critical issue, particularly in developing countries where two‑wheeled vehicles are disproportionately involved in crashes. This study evaluates the Motorcycle Collision‑Alert and Management System (MCAMS), a low‑cost aftermarket forward collision warning system, using a Naturalistic Driving Study with six riders in Jakarta, Depok, and Bogor, Indonesia. MCAMS continuously recorded kinematics, headway, time-to-collision, and front-view videos. Eighteen types of Safety‑Critical Events (SCE) were identified, Pooled SCE counts were lower after system activation (205 vs. 113), but the prespecified rider-level exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the six paired riders was not statistically significant, and the exposure-adjusted rate ratio was imprecise. Descriptively, lower counts were concentrated in scenarios such as tailgating and overtaking, whereas intersection and lateral conflicts showed little change, a pattern consistent with the system's forward-facing design. These results should be interpreted with caution, because this study used the small sample of six riders and the sequential pre–post design without a control group or randomized exposure. These preliminary findings support further investigation with larger samples, longer observation periods, and controlled exposure conditions to establish generalizability and causal inference.

title: Exploring the Drivers and Barriers for Circular Economy Implementation in the Mining Industry: An ISM Approach
summary: Mining is an important sector in the development of Indonesian and world civilization. With the largest-ever record of waste volumes and the potential for significant environmental impact, the industry is under constant pressure to maintain
content: Mining is an important sector in the development of Indonesian and world civilization. With the largest-ever record of waste volumes and the potential for significant environmental impact, the industry is under constant pressure to maintain and improve environmental performance while remaining economically profitable. This can be achieved by implementing a circular economy. The circular economy is still in its infancy in this sector, and the driving forces and barriers for its implementation are unknown. This study aims to identify the key drivers and barriers and to understand the interactions between factors by using the interpretive structural modeling (ISM) method. This research identified 20 drivers, with the key being the existence of a clear national action plan and technical regulations, and 17 barriers, with the key barrier being the difficulty of incorporating the circular economy as the company's core business. These key factors will assist practitioners and decision-makers in understanding, overcoming, and utilizing them to implement a circular economy in their companies.

title: Impact of lanthanum- and cerium-based coagulants on the loads of rare earth elements discharged from wastewater treatment plants
summary: Rare Earth Elements (REEs) are technology-critical elements with broad applications in various fields. Due to the higher production of light REEs compared to heavy REEs, applications have been developed mainly for light REEs, including the
content: Rare Earth Elements (REEs) are technology-critical elements with broad applications in various fields. Due to the higher production of light REEs compared to heavy REEs, applications have been developed mainly for light REEs, including the use of lanthanum (La) and cerium (Ce) as chemical coagulants for the removal of phosphorus from wastewater. However, the retention of La and Ce originating from such applications in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) remains unclear. We, therefore, analyzed samples collected from three WWTPs using La/Ce-based coagulants and from the surrounding surface waters using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. A consistent enrichment of La and Ce relative to the other REEs was observed in the sludge samples, in the effluent of the WWTPs and in the downstream surface waters. A mass budget was established to trace the various inputs and outputs of REEs in and out of the WWTPs. Our results show that >98% of the La and Ce input into the WWTP originated from the coagulant. The emitted La and Ce ranged from 2.1 · 10 –3 to 6.7 · 10 –2 g La /day/capita and from 1.1 · 10 –3 to 3.5 · 10 –2 g Ce /day/capita, respectively. These emissions were 2–3 orders of magnitude higher than the corresponding per capita emissions of La and Ce calculated for a control WWTP that exclusively used iron-based coagulants. At the highest concentrations of La and Ce observed in receiving waters, adverse effects on organisms cannot be excluded. Results from single-particle inductively coupled plasma time of flight mass spectrometry documented the release of nanoparticulate La and Ce, most likely in the form of nanoscale REE phosphates, from the WWTP.

title: Measuring multidimensional housing pressure in equitable and resilient Australian cities
summary: Housing equity is central to resilient, inclusive and sustainable urban development. Yet housing policy is often framed narrowly around prices, rents, supply shortages or individual affordability stress. This paper develops the concept of c
content: Housing equity is central to resilient, inclusive and sustainable urban development. Yet housing policy is often framed narrowly around prices, rents, supply shortages or individual affordability stress. This paper develops the concept of common-good housing pressure to capture the spatial concentration of housing conditions that affect not only households, but also the wider functioning of cities. Drawing on debates about housing equity, accessibility, spatial inequality and urban resilience, the paper constructs a small-area diagnostic for Australian capital cities using Statistical Area Level 2 (SA2) data. The index combines indicators of rental and mortgage stress, overcrowding, tenure exposure, socio-economic disadvantage, key-worker residence, service accessibility, development intensity, residential mobility and market exposure. The results show that high-pressure areas are not defined by affordability stress alone. Very high-pressure SA2s combine higher housing stress, substantially greater overcrowding, larger renter shares, lower socio-economic status, higher recent-arrival shares, greater population mobility, stronger development intensity and higher market/mobility exposure. Spatial autocorrelation analysis further shows that pressure is clustered, especially in Sydney and Melbourne, where hot spots form broader zones of metropolitan stress. The paper argues that housing equity is part of the social infrastructure of urban resilience. Policy responses therefore need to move beyond aggregate supply targets to place-sensitive interventions that secure affordable, adequate, and well-located housing in areas where housing conditions shape access to opportunity, workforce stability, and inclusive urban development.

title: Plankton ecological complexity amplifies climate-driven weakening of the ocean biological pump
summary: The ocean biological pump regulates atmospheric carbon dioxide, yet Earth system projections may miss how plankton food-web complexity shapes its response to warming. Here we use a single Earth system model framework with three progressivel
content: The ocean biological pump regulates atmospheric carbon dioxide, yet Earth system projections may miss how plankton food-web complexity shapes its response to warming. Here we use a single Earth system model framework with three progressively more complex plankton ecosystems to show that ecological complexity amplifies the climate-driven weakening of future carbon export. Across historical and future emission scenarios, warming and stratification cause only modest changes in global net primary production but persistent declines in net community production and export fluxes. This weakening increases systematically with ecosystem complexity across scenarios. Under SSP5-8.5, late-century global net community production falls by 5.8% in the default configuration, compared with 8.8% and 12.8% in the more complex configurations. The amplification arises from climate-driven shifts towards smaller phytoplankton and stronger zooplankton grazing, retaining more fixed carbon in the upper ocean. Coarse plankton representations may therefore underestimate future biological-pump weakening and climate-carbon feedbacks.

title: Particle removal by wet spraying scrubbers: an experimental study in a municipal waste incineration plant
summary: Given the health and environmental risks posed by particulate matter and ongoing regulatory efforts to reduce industrial emissions, this study investigated the particle removal efficiency of a downscaled wet spraying scrubber installed at a
content: Given the health and environmental risks posed by particulate matter and ongoing regulatory efforts to reduce industrial emissions, this study investigated the particle removal efficiency of a downscaled wet spraying scrubber installed at a municipal waste incineration plant. The scrubber was fed with a fraction of the flue gas, and particle mass and number concentrations were measured at the inlet and outlet to evaluate its performance and characterize the particles. The metal and carbon contents of the particles, as well as their capacity to induce oxidative stress, were analyzed to determine their chemical composition and toxicity. Scanning electron microscopy was used to assess particle morphology. Fractional removal efficiencies were calculated from upstream and downstream number-based particle size distributions. The scrubber was operated under 9 operating conditions to identify factors influencing its performance. Across all conditions, most particles were submicron-sized (mode ∼0.3 µm). Their carbon content was <1 wt%, while Na and K dominated (∼10 wt% each). Larger particles showed higher oxidative potential and metal content. Particle removal efficiency were higher (>90%) with small droplet sizes (nominal D 32 of 97 µm) and high liquid-to-gas flow ratios (10 L·m −3 ), whereas gas-spray contact time had no observed effect (between 4 and 10 s), for particles between 0.3 and 7 µm. These findings provide useful insights for developing guidelines on particulate emission mitigation and gas–liquid transfer in waste incineration.

title: Lignin-Based Adhesives for Wood-Based Panels: Bonding Pathways, Panel Performance, Sustainability Assessment and Industrial Readiness
summary: Purpose of Review Lignin is an abundant renewable aromatic polymer with considerable potential to reduce the dependence of wood-based panels on fossil-derived adhesives. This review, focused on literature published between 2019 and 2026, ex
content: Purpose of Review Lignin is an abundant renewable aromatic polymer with considerable potential to reduce the dependence of wood-based panels on fossil-derived adhesives. This review, focused on literature published between 2019 and 2026, examines how technical lignin characteristics, modification strategies and bonding mechanisms influence the manufacture and performance of particleboard, fibreboard, oriented strand board, plywood and panels produced from agricultural lignocellulosic residues. Particular attention is given to the translation of adhesive chemistry into panel-level performance, emissions, process compatibility, sustainability and industrial readiness. Recent Findings Lignin can contribute to panel bonding through partial substitution in phenol–formaldehyde and urea–formaldehyde resins, hybrid crosslinking, formaldehyde-free adhesive systems, direct addition to lignocellulosic furnish and native self-bonding. Moderate lignin substitution and hybrid systems currently provide the most consistent balance between renewable content, curing behaviour, mechanical performance and dimensional stability. Chemical activation, purification and fractionation can improve lignin reactivity and permit higher substitution levels, but also increase processing complexity, energy use and cost. Lignosulfonate-rich and binderless systems can produce panels with satisfactory mechanical properties, although moisture resistance, binder loading, pretreatment severity and pressing time frequently remain limiting factors. Reduced formaldehyde release is commonly reported, but complete volatile-organic-compound profiles and industrial-scale validation remain scarce. Environmental assessments further show that renewable lignin content alone does not guarantee lower impacts because lignin recovery, modification, co-reactants and panel processing can dominate the overall profile. Summary Lignin has progressed from a potential phenol substitute to a versatile platform for several panel-binding strategies. Near-term industrial adoption is most likely through moderate substitution and hybrid formulations compatible with existing production lines. Further advances to reach industrial implementation require performance-based lignin specifications, realistic pressing conditions, improved moisture durability, pilot and factory trials, and integrated life-cycle and techno-economic assessment of functionally equivalent panels.

title: Balancing Food and Climate: A Meta-Analysis of Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Rice Yield under Organic and Inorganic Amendments
summary: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from rice cultivation, particularly methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), pose significant challenges to climate change mitigation practices while maintaining food security. Management practices involving org
content: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from rice cultivation, particularly methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), pose significant challenges to climate change mitigation practices while maintaining food security. Management practices involving organic and inorganic amendment play a crucial role in regulating these emissions as well as influencing rice yield. However, the effects reported across studies remain inconsistent and context dependent. This meta-analysis aims to quantitatively synthesize existing evidence to evaluate the impacts of organic and inorganic amendments on CH4 and N2O emissions and yield outcomes from rice fields. The findings will provide insights into sustainable input management strategies for balancing productivity with environmental goals. Also, most of the studies did not include all the parameters such as nutrient availability, GHGs emissions, and yield attributes. Thus, we try to establish a concrete link in-between. PICO • Population (P): Paddy (rice) fields / rice cropping systems (field experiments, lysimeter/plot studies, chamber measurements). • Intervention (I): Organic amendments (manure, compost, crop residues, biochar when used as amendment) OR inorganic amendments (mineral fertilizers, NPK, urea, ammonium sulfate, etc.). • Comparison (C): Organic vs inorganic amendments; amended vs unamended; different amendment rates/types. • Outcomes (O): Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions — methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂) fluxes (fluxes, cumulative emissions, emission factors), and crop yield (grain yield, biomass). Secondary: global warming potential (GWP), yield-scaled GHG emissions.

title: KarbunWise is a climate intelligence and sustainability platform that helps businesses measure, manage, reduce, and report their environmental impact. It combines AI-powered software with expert advisory services across carbon accounting, ESG management, Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), climate risk, and decarbonisation. The platform supports Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions tracking, supplier engagement, net-zero planning, and compliance with frameworks such as CSRD, BRSR, GRI, CDP, and SBTi. Serving industries including manufacturing, construction, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, textiles, and IT, KarbunWise simplifies sustainability data management, automates reporting, and delivers actionable insights to help organisations achieve measurable climate goals and build a sustainable future.

content: As businesses face increasing pressure to address climate change, reduce carbon emissions, and meet environmental regulations, sustainability has become an essential part of business strategy. KarbunWise is helping organisations navigate this transition through innovative climate intelligence solutions, advanced technology, and expert sustainability consulting. Making Sustainability Simple and Measurable KarbunWise combines intelligent software with professional expertise to help organisations understand and improve their environmental performance.
