Meanwhile, cement exports more than doubled and aluminium exports increased by about 60%, while there is no contraction specific to EU destinations. Also, there is no contraction in Egypt and Brazil, which are heavily exposed to CBAM. The results indicate that the description of CBAM as a “homogenous trade shock” cannot be justified based on the findings. The differences in sectors can be explained by the variety of carbon intensities, production technologies, company sizes, adaptive capacities, logistics costs, and policies across the different countries. Policy implications include the application of Climate Law No. 7552 in Türkiye, assistance to small exporters, the strengthening of emissions data infrastructure, and the accounting for modernization in the context of the EU-Türkiye Customs Union. This paper presents one of the earliest ex-post comparative analyses of Turkish exports in the context of CBAM. By employing the country comparison approach, validation through proxies, falsification checks, and the analysis of logistics costs, it provides a replicable model that contributes to the predominantly ex-ante CBAM literature.

title: AI words, AI deeds, and environmental assessment: the role of managerial ability
source: International Journal of Climate Change Strategies and Management
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how managerial ability (MA), AI-related disclosure (AI Words) and AI-related investment intensity (AI Deeds), a CSMAR-based proxy covering enabling digital assets, relate to composite environmental perform
content: Purpose This study aims to examine how managerial ability (MA), AI-related disclosure (AI Words) and AI-related investment intensity (AI Deeds), a CSMAR-based proxy covering enabling digital assets, relate to composite environmental performance (EP) and external environmental ratings and whether the two AI measures are assessed differently. Design/methodology/approach Using data from Chinese non-financial A-share listed firms for 2010–2023, the study estimates models with firm and year fixed effects to examine the associations of MA, AI Words and AI Deeds with EP and external environmental ratings. Findings MA has a modest positive association with EP and a consistent negative association with AI Deeds, although the corresponding indirect association remains exploratory. In the contemporaneous model for the full rated sample, AI Words is associated with higher external ratings and AI Deeds with lower ratings, while neither is associated with rating-excluded EP. This pattern indicates a potential environmental assessment gap. Practical implications Regulators, rating providers and boards may benefit from distinguishing visible AI narratives from verifiable implementation and outcomes. Assessment and oversight frameworks for climate-transition governance could consider disclosure, resource allocation and energy implications rather than treating AI adoption as uniformly beneficial. Such alignment may also strengthen the credibility of sustainability information, stakeholder trust and corporate accountability. Originality/value Building on words–deeds, symbolic–substantive and AI-washing research, this study extends the words–deeds distinction to environmental assessment and positions MA as a governance-related resource-orchestration factor while recognising the measurement sensitivity of the MA–EP evidence.

title: Advancing Canada’s energy future: a systematic-descriptive review of CCUS and blue hydrogen for environmental sustainability
summary: Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) and blue hydrogen are increasingly considered potential components of industrial decarbonization strategies, yet the associated evidence remains fragmented across technological, environmental,
content: Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) and blue hydrogen are increasingly considered potential components of industrial decarbonization strategies, yet the associated evidence remains fragmented across technological, environmental, economic, infrastructure, and policy dimensions. This study conducts a systematic descriptive review of journal articles, review articles, and conference papers published between 2015 and 2026, sourced from Web of Science and ScienceDirect, to critically assess the role of CCUS and blue hydrogen in advancing Canada's environmental sustainability and net-zero objectives. The evidence indicates that the environmental performance of blue hydrogen depends heavily on production technology, CO2-capture performance, upstream methane emissions, energy inputs, and lifecycle system boundaries. In one directly comparable steam methane reforming assessment, integrating ≥ 95% CO2 capture reduced lifecycle emissions from 11.99 to 6.59 kgCO2e/kgH2, while a separate oil-sands fuel-substitution study reported a 76% emissions reduction under a different system boundary. Comparisons with green hydrogen depend on electricity source, technology, geography, and lifecycle boundaries. Renewable electrolysis typically shows lower climate impacts than fossil-based methods when using low-carbon electricity. Economic viability varies by context, with studies indicating a $99/t CO2 profitability threshold for oil sands and a $300/t CO2 threshold at which the marginal abatement cost of hydrogen blending becomes negative. Overall, the evidence supports blue hydrogen as a conditional transitional decarbonization option, particularly for hard-to-abate Canadian sectors with suitable CCUS infrastructure, rather than as an inherently low-carbon or universally preferable pathway. The review identifies harmonized lifecycle assessment, methane control, infrastructure development, social and Indigenous engagement, and comparative evaluation of alternative decarbonization pathways as priorities for future research and policy.

title: Carbon dioxide responses shape estimates of Amazon forest vulnerability under solar geoengineering
summary: The Amazon rainforest is vulnerable to warming and changes in rainfall, yet whether solar geoengineering can reduce conditions associated with forest loss remains uncertain. Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) can offset greenhouse-gas-dr
content: The Amazon rainforest is vulnerable to warming and changes in rainfall, yet whether solar geoengineering can reduce conditions associated with forest loss remains uncertain. Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) can offset greenhouse-gas-driven warming without fully restoring regional hydroclimate. Here we assess Amazon forest vulnerability under mitigation, high-emission and SAI scenarios using a CO₂-dependent forest-sustainability threshold in a common climate phase space. By late century, SAI reduces projected Amazon warming from 5.49 °C under high emissions to 2.45 °C, but substantial drying and longer dry seasons persist. Under SAI, 44.7% of analysed grid cells exceed the present-day threshold, compared with 8.7% when the future CO₂-dependent threshold is considered. This contrast reveals that apparent forest protection depends strongly on the assumed resilience benefits of elevated CO₂. Our findings highlight the importance of hydroclimatic changes and CO₂-dependent vegetation responses in assessing the potential of solar geoengineering to reduce Amazon forest vulnerability.

title: Does inequality harm the climate? An agent-based model with endogenous climate policy
summary: This paper examines how income inequality affects environmental outcomes through the interplay of household consumption and political support for climate policy. We develop an agent-based model in which households differ by income, consumpt
content: This paper examines how income inequality affects environmental outcomes through the interplay of household consumption and political support for climate policy. We develop an agent-based model in which households differ by income, consumption patterns, and climate policy attitudes. Our results show that the relationship between inequality and emissions is dynamic and non-monotonic: relative to a baseline calibrated to the U.S., lower income inequality initially increases emissions due to rising consumption among formerly low-income households. Over time, however, reduced inequality fosters broader political support for tighter climate action, as a more equal income distribution lowers the relative cost of carbon taxation for households at the bottom of the distribution. This stronger support enables more ambitious policies and ultimately reduces emissions. Moreover, we find that lower inequality consistently produces the lowest cumulative emissions across scenarios. The findings highlight the importance of distributional considerations in designing effective and politically sustainable climate policies.

title: Self-Sufficiency as a Political Virtue: Agency and Responsibility in the Age of Technology
summary: Contemporary political philosophy has devoted extensive attention to technology, risk, and governance, yet it has paid little attention to the role of everyday material practices in shaping political virtue under industrial conditions. This
content: Contemporary political philosophy has devoted extensive attention to technology, risk, and governance, yet it has paid little attention to the role of everyday material practices in shaping political virtue under industrial conditions. This paper argues that an increased degree of self-sufficiency, understood as domain-sensitive reduction of market reliance, should be recovered as a political virtue for technologically mediated societies. While acknowledging the benefits of industrial society like abundance and health security, the paper diagnoses how large-scale production and radical division of labour generate social exploitation, ecological harm, and individual alienation. Calibrated self-sufficiency is defended as a practical response that reduces social and ecological complicity while preserving opportunities for materially engaged agency and forms of activity that may be conducive to flourishing. The argument frames self-sufficiency as a context-sensitive optimization strategy, demonstrating that this orientation is universalizable without requiring social withdrawal or technological regression.

title: Potential alternative sustainable feedstocks for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in Indonesia
summary: The global energy transition has established Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) as a key option for aviation decarbonisation. Indonesia has substantial potential to develop Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA)-based SAF because of its
content: The global energy transition has established Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) as a key option for aviation decarbonisation. Indonesia has substantial potential to develop Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA)-based SAF because of its large aviation market and diverse lipid resources. This study identifies and prioritizes technically and economically feasible feedstocks using literature review, stakeholder Focus Group Discussions and interviews, SWOT analysis, a study-specific feedstock-to-refinery-gate greenhouse-gas assessment informed by CORSIA life-cycle accounting principles, and financial evaluation using Net Present Value, Benefit-Cost Ratio, and Internal Rate of Return. This integrated framework provides a distinctive assessment of alternative HEFA feedstocks by linking stakeholder-based prioritization with environmental and economic performance under Indonesian supply-chain conditions. Fourteen alternative feedstocks were screened, with Used Cooking Oil (UCO) included as a benchmark. The integrated assessment identifies PFAD and Non-Standard Coconut (NSC) as short-term strategic options, with beef tallow and UCO offering medium-term potential subject to supply and allocation arrangements, while Calophyllum inophyllum L. and Pongamia pinnata represent longer-term cultivation-based options. The study-specific feedstock-to-refinery-gate GHG intensities are 12.95 gCO₂e/MJ for UCO, 12.73–13.11 gCO₂e/MJ for PFAD, 28.29 gCO₂e/MJ for beef tallow, 18.77–18.95 gCO₂e/MJ for Calophyllum inophyllum L., 60.45 gCO₂e/MJ for NSC, and 36.84–37.31 gCO₂e/MJ for Pongamia pinnata. Where available, the study-specific results are compared with current CORSIA default core LCA values as external benchmarks; the calculated values are reported as study-specific screening estimates rather than certified CORSIA Actual Life Cycle Emissions values. Preliminary economic analysis indicates that PFAD and NSC have the highest NPV, while all assessed feedstocks have a Benefit-Cost Ratio above 1.

title: Beyond trophic interactions: multidimensional plant–bird interaction networks in a tropical urban ecosystem
summary: Urban ecosystems can modify plant–bird interactions by altering plant community composition, vegetation structure, and the availability of food, nesting substrates, perching sites, and nest-building materials. Although most studies have foc
content: Urban ecosystems can modify plant–bird interactions by altering plant community composition, vegetation structure, and the availability of food, nesting substrates, perching sites, and nest-building materials. Although most studies have focused on trophic relationships such as frugivory or pollination, the simultaneous integration of trophic and non-trophic interactions in urban environments remains poorly understood. In this study, we quantified five types of plant–bird interactions (feeding, perching, preening, nesting, and provisioning of nesting material) on the campus of Universidad CES (Medellín, Colombia) to evaluate their joint structure using ecological network analysis. Over three years, we recorded 2,780 plant–bird interaction events. After consolidating repeated observations by bird species, plant taxon, and interaction type, these events corresponded to 866 unique interactions involving 112 plant taxa and 71 bird species. The complete network exhibited a significant modular pattern (Q = 0.31; p < 0.01), with 12 plant taxa acting as key elements for connectivity. Among these key taxa, Cecropia angustifolia and Guadua angustifolia were particularly notable because they were involved in all five interaction types. Specialization varied among interaction types, with nesting showing the highest value (H 2 ′ = 0.913), followed by provisioning of nesting material (H 2 ′ = 0.599), feeding (H 2 ′ = 0.552), preening (H 2 ′ = 0.378), and perching (H 2 ′ = 0.257). These findings demonstrate that integrating multiple interaction types allows the identification of plant taxa that play differentiated functional roles in urban landscapes. Identifying these key taxa provides valuable tools for green infrastructure planning and avifauna conservation in tropical cities.

title: Carbon Monitor: Global 0.1° Monthly Greenhouse Gas and Air Pollutant Emissions across 35 Sectors, 2019–September 2026
summary: This dataset provides global monthly gridded emissions at 0.1° resolution from 1 January 2019 to 30 September 2026. It covers three greenhouse gases—carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O)—and seven air pollutants and pr
content: This dataset provides global monthly gridded emissions at 0.1° resolution from 1 January 2019 to 30 September 2026. It covers three greenhouse gases—carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O)—and seven air pollutants and precursors: black carbon (BC), organic carbon (OC), carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxides (NOx), sulfur dioxide (SO2), ammonia (NH3) and non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs).The core product uses a consistent classification of 35 source sectors, comprising three power categories, 21 industry categories, four ground transport categories, four residential and other fuel-use categories, and one category each for domestic aviation, international aviation and international shipping. Coal, oil and gas fugitive CH4 emissions are included as supplementary components. N2O estimates include biomass combustion within the covered sectors.Monthly emissions are calculated from the underlying daily estimates and expressed as kilograms per grid cell per month. BC and OC are reported as carbon mass, NOx as NO2 mass, and the remaining species as the mass of the respective compound. Data are provided in compressed NetCDF format. Integer-packed variables must be decoded using the spatially varying scaling information stored in the files, as explained in the accompanying documentation.The product covers the specified energy, industrial, transport and other fuel-use sources. Non-combustion agricultural emissions, waste and natural sources, and the separate nitric- and adipic-acid production sources of N2O are outside the present coverage. Gas-flaring CO2 is not separately resolved.The public release includes monthly gridded emissions, supporting daily country-sector emission time series, and source data underlying the associated figures. The full daily gridded dataset is available from the corresponding author upon request. These data support analyses of emission trends, sectoral and regional contributions, climate mitigation, and air-quality co-benefits.

title: Bio-based pine resin processing in Indonesia: Environmental impacts, carbon storage potential, and climate mitigation implications of gum rosin production
summary: This study assessed the environmental impacts of gum rosin production from pine resin, a prominent non-timber forest product in Indonesia, identified key emission hotspots, and compared its environmental impacts and carbon storage potential
content: This study assessed the environmental impacts of gum rosin production from pine resin, a prominent non-timber forest product in Indonesia, identified key emission hotspots, and compared its environmental impacts and carbon storage potential with substitute products. The ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint method, integrated with the ecoinvent 3 database, was employed using primary data from company records and interviews conducted over a three-year period (2020–2022). The system boundary was cradle-to-gate, applying economic allocation among co-products including firewood, logs, and turpentine oil. The functional unit was 1 tonne of gum rosin. Overall, forest operations producing fresh pine resin were the main contributors to most environmental impact categories, primarily due to the use of paint, solvents, and resin stimulants. However, when factory activities were aggregated, manufacturing accounted for over 47% of total impacts, mainly from electrogalvanized steel drum packaging and electricity consumption. A comparative analysis of global warming indicated that gum rosin had lower impacts than substitute materials used in paper sizing, adhesives, and rubber compounding. Furthermore, its carbon storage potential was comparable to values reported in studies from several regions, underscoring its environmental advantages. The results indicated that forest operations and the manufacturing stage are priority areas for improvement. Recommended strategies include replacing paint and resin stimulants with lower-impact alternatives, such as waterborne conventional paints or plant-based stimulants, adopting reusable gum rosin packaging and optimizing energy consumption. The findings support strategies for enhancing the sustainability of the gum rosin industry and provide a basis for future research on downstream products.

title: From Accession Conditionality to Market Imperatives: The Politics of Carbon Border Adjustment and EU–Turkey Climate Convergence
source: JCMS Journal of Common Market Studies
summary: This article examines Turkey's 2025 Climate Law as a case of European Union (EU) external governance after accession conditionality declined. Using theory‐guided process tracing and analysis of legislation, debates, documents and stakeholde
content: This article examines Turkey's 2025 Climate Law as a case of European Union (EU) external governance after accession conditionality declined. Using theory‐guided process tracing and analysis of legislation, debates, documents and stakeholder positions, it traces how the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism altered the costs of regulatory non‐alignment. The findings identify a transmission–transformation gap: market‐access incentives accelerated adoption of an EU‐compatible legal and institutional framework, including an emissions trading system mandate, without comparable change in costly areas such as coal phase‐out, interim targets and limits on executive discretion. The article distinguishes the Brussels Effect as external regulatory transmission, Europeanisation as the depth of domestic change and external differentiated integration as the institutional form of selective alignment. It describes this pattern as defensive integration: instrumental adaptation driven by the need to limit economic losses whilst preserving domestic policy autonomy. Developments through August 2026 indicate institutional development, but implementation outcomes remain unresolved.

title: Synthesis and Reliability of Emerging Atomic Layer Deposited Ferroelectric Thin Films for Microelectronics
summary: Ferroelectrics present an attractive candidate for non volatile memory (NVM) as they exhibit a spontaneous polarization whose orientation can be reversed with an electric field. Ferroelectric NVM technologies provide advantages in cost per
content: Ferroelectrics present an attractive candidate for non volatile memory (NVM) as they exhibit a spontaneous polarization whose orientation can be reversed with an electric field. Ferroelectric NVM technologies provide advantages in cost per memory bit, read/write times, and power efficiency; however, conventional perovskite ferroelectrics preclude integration in modern semiconductor technologies due to challenging dimensional scaling and complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) compatibility. In the 21st century, two new families of ferroelectrics have emerged: fluorites and wurtzites. Although fluorite and wurtzite structured ferroelectrics can circumvent the current issues limiting integration of perovskites, they pose new challenges in synthesis and reliability. The first topic in this dissertation is the retention performance of ferroelectric Hf1 xZrxO2 (HZO) thin films. Polarization retention is a critical issue limiting widespread implementation of ferroelectric NVM in microelectronics. In ferroelectric NVM, opposite polarization orientations serve as the binary logic states “1” and “0”; therefore, retention of the polarization state is necessary to ensure that memory remains non volatile. The retention performance of HZO thin films is highly sensitive to the capping electrode chemistry; however, the underlying mechanism of this has not been studied prior to this work. Electrodes that undergo greater chemical reactions with the HZO layer (such as TaN) exhibit poorer polarization retention than more inert electrodes (such as W). Reactive electrodes lead to thicker interfacial layers and increased oxygen scavenging of the HZO layer, which contribute to increased imprint and a decreased opposite state polarization margin. This suggests that using inert electrode chemistries (such as W) will improve the reliability of ferroelectric HZO for NVM applications through suppression of interfacial reactions. The second topic in this dissertation is focused on the atomic layer deposition (ALD) of ferroelectric Zn1 xMgxO (ZMO). To date, synthesis of ferroelectric wurtzites (including ZMO) has primarily been conducted using line of sight growth methods such as sputtering and molecular beam epitaxy. High density ferroelectric NVM requires 3D architectures with high aspect ratios, which necessitates the ability to grow these materials using ALD. Process development of ALD ZnO and ALD MgO growth is conducted to enable growth of ALD ZMO. Following this, ferroelectric switching in ALD ZMO thin films is observed for compositions of x = 0.46 and 0.58. Furthermore, the impact of composition on the structure and defects in ALD ZMO is investigated. Mg containing ZMO thin films (x > 0) largely exhibit composition independent luminescence, defect energies, and bulk conduction activation energies. title: Limited emission reduction from China’s low-carbon city pilot: evidence from 112 Yangtze River Economic Belt Cities
summary: China’s Low-Carbon City Pilot (LCCP) program covers 72 of 112 prefecture-level cities in the Yangtze River Economic Belt (YREB) across three staggered cohorts (2010, 2012, 2017) and is among the world’s largest subnational climate experimen
content: China’s Low-Carbon City Pilot (LCCP) program covers 72 of 112 prefecture-level cities in the Yangtze River Economic Belt (YREB) across three staggered cohorts (2010, 2012, 2017) and is among the world’s largest subnational climate experiments. Using a balanced panel of 1,870 city-year observations (2007–2023) and two-way fixed effects with city-clustered standard errors, we find no statistically significant effect of LCCP on CO₂ emissions ( β = 0.032, p = 0.256). Event-study estimates find no strong evidence against parallel pretreatment trends (joint Wald χ²=7.316, p = 0.120), while post-treatment coefficients turn significantly negative only after seven to nine years (k = 7: −0.120, p = 0.011; k = 8: −0.111, p = 0.038; k = 9: −0.142, p = 0.015). A dose–response analysis confirms this pattern: each additional exposure year is associated with a 1.1% reduction in CO₂ emissions ( β =−0.011, p = 0.043). Heterogeneity across cohorts, regions, and city size is imprecise, and a descriptive decomposition attributes part of the association to carbon intensity, a near-definitional channel that cannot support causal claims. An interaction analysis finds no evidence that carbon trading amplified the effect (interaction β = 0.010, p = 0.878). After 17 years, the LCCP program has produced no detectable emission reduction across YREB cities, although delayed, dose-dependent reductions may materialize over a decade or more, calling for extended evaluation timelines.

title: Subcritical-water carbon-dot framework: reproducible data, code, and prediction notebook
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Reproducible computational archive accompanying the Nanoscale article “Predicting carbon-dot emission centers and quantum yield from subcritical-water state: a reproducible multiscale computational framework”. Contents. The SI-locked anchor
content: Reproducible computational archive accompanying the Nanoscale article “Predicting carbon-dot emission centers and quantum yield from subcritical-water state: a reproducible multiscale computational framework”. Contents. The SI-locked anchor tables (CSV) for liquid density, the static dielectric constant, dynamic viscosity, the ionic product (pKw) and saturation pressure; the out-of-sample blind-test data; fixed random seeds; a dependency lock; the analysis scripts (Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation, Morris sensitivity, continuum reaction-field coupling, multi-source cross-validation and two out-of-sample tests); a reliability layer comprising leave-one-out cross-validation with 95% prediction-interval coverage (c1_loocv.py), a three-input solvent-state decision map with region A/B/C boundaries (c2_decision_map.py), and a multi-system confusion-matrix summary of the out-of-sample tests (c3_confusion_matrix.py); and a minimal NumPy-only notebook that returns a prediction from three process inputs (temperature, fill ratio, hold time). Anchors. Fifteen density and dielectric states from 25 to 350 °C, densified across the 180–220 °C window and toward the critical point. The dielectric constant is computed from the IAPWS R8-97 formulation (e.g. ε = 31.50 at 220 °C); density, pressure and viscosity follow IAPWS-95/R12-08 and the ionic product follows R11-24. Reproduction. Fixed seeds with NumPy 1.26.4 on Python 3.12 reproduce the sampled values bit-for-bit; the notebook uses NumPy only and raises on inputs outside the validated ranges. Scope. Anchor values are interpolations of the IAPWS/NIST releases documented in the manuscript and supporting information, and the continuum reaction-field quantities are analytic. No quantum-chemical (DFT/PCM) or REFPROP/SUPCRT output is included because those packages were not run. License. Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY-4.0).

title: Multiobjective stochastic integer programming for lunar colony transportation optimization
source: International Conference on Machine Learning, Neural Networks, and Computer Software (MLNNCS)
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive multi-objective stochastic integer programming framework for optimizing transportation systems in lunar colony construction. We address the fundamental challenge of delivering approximately 100 million to
content: This paper presents a comprehensive multi-objective stochastic integer programming framework for optimizing transportation systems in lunar colony construction. We address the fundamental challenge of delivering approximately 100 million tons of construction materials and operational supplies to establish a sustainable lunar settlement capable of supporting 100,000 inhabitants. Three distinct transportation architectures are systematically evaluated: traditional launch vehicle systems utilizing chemical propulsion, emerging space elevator technology based on advanced carbon nanotube tethers, and hybrid approaches strategically combining both methods. Our stochastic optimization model explicitly incorporates realistic operational uncertainties including equipment failures, performance degradation over time, launch success probabilities, and environmental variability. The framework simultaneously optimizes three competing objectives: minimizing total mission cost, reducing construction timeline, and limiting environmental impact measured through comprehensive carbon emission accounting. Computational experiments conducted using genetic algorithms with Monte Carlo simulation demonstrate that the hybrid transportation scheme achieves superior Paretooptimal solutions, reducing carbon emissions by over 54% compared to pure launch vehicle approaches while maintaining economically and temporally feasible construction schedules. Extensive sensitivity analysis validates the robustness of our conclusions under various parameter perturbations including elevator capacity degradation rates, launch reliability variations, and demand fluctuations. This research provides rigorous quantitative decision support for future large-scale space infrastructure development and contributes methodological advances in stochastic multiobjective optimization for complex aerospace systems.

title: Revisiting the FDI, Industrialization and Environmental Pollution Nexus: The Conditional Role of Renewable Energy in Developing Economies
summary: This study examines how foreign direct investment (FDI) and industrialization (IND) affect carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions and whether renewable energy (REN) alters these relationships. Using a balanced panel of 101 d
content: This study examines how foreign direct investment (FDI) and industrialization (IND) affect carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions and whether renewable energy (REN) alters these relationships. Using a balanced panel of 101 developing countries from 2002 to 2022, the analysis applies two-way fixed effects with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, two-step System GMM, and Lewbel IV–2SLS. The results consistently show that FDI and IND increase both pollutants, supporting the Pollution Haven Hypothesis, whereas REN directly reduces emissions. The negative interaction effects indicate that REN significantly weakens the adverse environmental effects of FDI and IND. Marginal-effects analysis shows that these effects remain positive at low and median REN levels but become small and generally statistically insignificant at the 75th percentile. The estimated zero-crossing thresholds range from approximately 66.6% to 78.6% of total final energy consumption, suggesting that substantial REN penetration is required to neutralize the pollution effects of foreign investment and industrial expansion. Institutional-quality heterogeneity analysis further reveals that stronger institutions reduce the emission intensity of FDI and IND and enhance the direct and moderating benefits of REN. These findings reconcile the Pollution Haven and Pollution Halo hypotheses by demonstrating that the environmental consequences of economic expansion depend on energy structure and institutional capacity. Developing countries should therefore coordinate renewable-energy expansion with environmental regulation, green-investment screening, and cleaner industrial policies.

title: Recent Decline in Global Atmospheric COS Driven By Reduced Anthropogenic CS2 Emissions
summary: Carbonyl sulfide (COS or OCS) is an atmospheric trace gas which is a tracer for carbon cycle processes. Previous work suggests that anthropogenic carbon disulfide (CS2) emissions from viscose rayon production are the primary control of deca
content: Carbonyl sulfide (COS or OCS) is an atmospheric trace gas which is a tracer for carbon cycle processes. Previous work suggests that anthropogenic carbon disulfide (CS2) emissions from viscose rayon production are the primary control of decadal trends in global COS mixing ratios. However, the potential influence of these anthropogenic sources on a recently observed decline in atmospheric COS have yet to be studied. Here we analyze viscose rayon emissions and assess their contributions to atmospheric COS using atmospheric abundance observations and simulations. We found that COS decreases from year 2016 to 2022 across globally-distributed sites. Unlike earlier periods when atmospheric COS and viscose rayon production were correlated, the 2016 to 2022 COS decline is counter to continued growth in viscose production. However, atmospheric simulations show that industrial emission factor reductions, noted in rayon industry reports, may be sufficient to explain the decrease in observed COS concentrations. This study emphasizes the role of viscose rayon production on the COS budget and provides evidence supporting a recent decline in global CS2 emissions.

title: A climate-resilient suitability framework for strategic offshore wind development in the Indian EEZ under CMIP6 climate scenarios
summary: Offshore wind is a key resource for the transition toward low-carbon energy systems. However, existing assessments inadequately address climate robustness and techno-environmental feasibility under future climate conditions. This study intr
content: Offshore wind is a key resource for the transition toward low-carbon energy systems. However, existing assessments inadequately address climate robustness and techno-environmental feasibility under future climate conditions. This study introduces an Offshore Wind Suitability Index (OWSI) to quantify the climate resilience of offshore wind resources. Near-surface winds from ten Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models were bias-adjusted against the fifth-generation European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) reanalysis (ERA5) using Weibull-based Quantile Mapping (QMW) for the historical period (1990–2014) and Weibull-based Quantile Delta Mapping (QDMW) for the projections, and the adjusted fields were combined into a median multi-model ensemble (MME). The corrected fields were used to derive eight indicators representing wind resource characteristics, variability, bathymetric suitability, and logistical feasibility. A hybrid multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) framework combining the Criteria Importance Through Inter-criteria Correlation (CRITIC) and Delphi methods determined indicator weights to develop the OWSI. The framework is demonstrated over the Indian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) across four sub-regions. Findings reveal pronounced spatial heterogeneity, with the north-eastern (NE) and north-western (NW) sectors consistently most favourable. Under the high-emission Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenario SSP5−8.5 in the far future (FF, 2076–2100), the highest (relative, quantile-based) suitability class expands by 33.6% and 45.6% relative to the historical baseline in the NE and NW sectors respectively, whereas the south-western (SW) sector declines. The framework identifies 56 plausible zones, including a location with an estimated installed capacity of 283.8 GW (an upper-bound, resource-driven estimate). The proposed approach provides a resource- and techno-economically informed screening framework for preliminary identification of climate-resilient offshore wind zones in India, prior to detailed marine spatial planning.

title: ENGINEERING SURVIVAL: HOW MERCEDES-BENZ IS REINVENTING ITS INDUSTRIAL AND ECONOMIC MODEL IN GERMANY TO FACE FUTURE CRISES A Strategic, Engineering, and Legal Reference for Decision Makers, Engineers, and Business Leaders
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This monograph provides a rigorous strategic, engineering, and legal analysis of how Mercedes-Benz is reinventing its industrial model to survive the existential crises facing German manufacturing. Targeted at C-suite executives, engineers,
content: This monograph provides a rigorous strategic, engineering, and legal analysis of how Mercedes-Benz is reinventing its industrial model to survive the existential crises facing German manufacturing. Targeted at C-suite executives, engineers, and policymakers, it dissects the collapse of traditional advantages due to energy shocks, bureaucratic rigidity, and agile global competitors. The book details Mercedes’ multi-dimensional counter-strategy: shifting from volume to ultra-luxury value, deploying hyper-flexible smart factories (Factory 56), reclaiming software sovereignty via MB.OS, and negotiating a new social contract using advanced labor law mechanisms like Transformation Clauses. Crucially, it addresses complex legal-geopolitical challenges, including navigating the US Inflation Reduction Act, EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, and strict liabilities under the EU AI Act and Scope 3 emissions mandates. Complete with actionable frameworks, resilience scorecards, and supply chain legal mitigation matrices, this work serves as a definitive operational playbook for protecting industrial bases through innovation, agility, and strategic foresight rather than protectionism. Digital Object Identifier: 10.5281/zenodo.24433869

title: Studying the Fullerene Nest: JWST Observations of the Planetary Nebula Tc 1. II. A Spectroscopic and Spatial Study of C60 and C70 Emission
summary: We present a detailed analysis of the fullerene emission bands in JWST MIRI/MRS observations of the planetary nebula Tc 1. The observations reveal the emission features due to neutral C60 and C70 in unprecedented detail. The combined fuller
content: We present a detailed analysis of the fullerene emission bands in JWST MIRI/MRS observations of the planetary nebula Tc 1. The observations reveal the emission features due to neutral C60 and C70 in unprecedented detail. The combined fullerene emission represents ∼2.6% of the total infrared output, suggesting that ∼0.6% of the carbon budget is locked up in fullerenes. We find no clear evidence for C+60, C+70 or C−60 in the spectrum. The high spectral resolution allows us to separate the fullerene bands from atomic emission lines for the first time, allowing for a much better characterization of the band profiles and yielding more accurate band ratios than previous observations. We see no spatial variation in the individual C60 and C70 band profile shapes across all pixels. The 17.4 and 18.9 μm C60 bands show clear resolved ro-vibrational structure in their profiles, and similar structured emission is seen in the 12.5, 14.8, 17.7, and 21.8 μm C70 bands, further establishing that all emitting fullerene molecules are in the gas phase. We report a higher 7.0/18.9 μm C60 band ratio (∼1.4-1.9) than previously reported (∼1.3). We note that all bands, except the 8.5 μm band, contain a significant contribution from C70, complicating the analysis. The fullerene emission is spatially concentrated in a thin, asymmetric shell at a radius of 5-6′′ from the central star. The shell lies at the outer edge of the core of the nebula, which was ejected in a single, brief episode ≳4,000 years ago.

title: Unprecedented role of tropical South American fires in the record atmospheric CO₂ growth in 2024
summary: In 2024, the global annual mean surface temperature rose above 1.5°C for the first time, coinciding with a record atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) growth rate. Using satellite carbon monoxide (CO) and CO2 observations in an atmospheric flux
content: In 2024, the global annual mean surface temperature rose above 1.5°C for the first time, coinciding with a record atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) growth rate. Using satellite carbon monoxide (CO) and CO2 observations in an atmospheric flux inversion framework, we attribute a substantial portion of this CO₂ growth anomaly to elevated fire emissions. Particularly, fires in tropical South America accounted for more than half of the global fire emission anomaly, contributing 766 ± 131 teragrams of carbon—the highest level since 2000. This fire surge, driven by exceptional heat and drought associated with the combined influence of El Niño and anomalous tropical North Atlantic warming, offset two decades of declining deforestation emissions. These findings highlight a strengthening fire–climate feedback, demonstrating how regional extremes increasingly shape the global carbon budget and complicate pathways to climate stabilization.

title: Addressing Indian textile industry transition to circular economy through consumer’s lens-systematic literature review
summary: The accelerating pace of industrialization and consumer-driven economic growth has intensified environmental degradation, posing serious risks to ecological stability and long-term human well-being. Indian textile industry, having a 3.9% sh
content: The accelerating pace of industrialization and consumer-driven economic growth has intensified environmental degradation, posing serious risks to ecological stability and long-term human well-being. Indian textile industry, having a 3.9% share of the global trade, substantially contributes to freshwater consumption, chemical pollution, carbon emissions, and solid waste generation. This industry employing ~45 million people uses ~ 1.6 million litres of water daily for processing 8000 kg of textile materials and therefore is attributed to almost 20% of all the freshwater pollution owing to toxic chemicals and dyes. Rapid expansion driven by globalization and fast fashion trends has further amplified pressures on freshwater resources and climate systems, directly undermining Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 6, 9, 12, and 13. Addressing these interconnected challenges requires an integrated approach that examines industrial production systems and the behavioral drivers of excessive consumption. Transitioning from a linear take–make–dispose model to a circular economy framework emphasizing reduction, reuse, recycling, and regeneration offers a viable pathway toward sustainability. However, effective implementation remains constrained by technological limitations, financial barriers, fragmented supply chains, and deeply entrenched consumer practices. This review work assesses the current scenario of textile industry from consumer’s perspective and aims to come up with steps required for the implementation of circular economy framework. A systematic literature with qualitative thematic synthesis was conducted using Google Scholar, employing predefined keywords related to circular economy, the Indian textile industry, consumer behavior, and textile pollution; 78 articles were initially identified, of which 60 relevant articles were selected and thematically synthesized across the pre-use, use, and post-use stages of textile consumption. After conducting the study, it can be said that by managing consumer behavior at the different stages of textile processing, significant improvements can be made for this transition. As consumer has significant impact on pre-use, use, and post-use stage of the textile, the awareness and actions of consumer helps in circularity of the product to huge extent. The analysis underscores that technological innovation must be complemented by consumer awareness for conscious purchase and usage, upbringing of desired infrastructure through responsible corporate and policy decisions.

title: Non-enzymatic assimilation of organosulfur compounds at the interface of geochemistry and biochemistry
summary: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) have important microbial-driven roles in global nutrient cycling, chemotaxis and/or climate regulation. Microbial DMSO and DMS assimilation were thought to require their enzymatic reducti
content: Dimethyl sulfide (DMS) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) have important microbial-driven roles in global nutrient cycling, chemotaxis and/or climate regulation. Microbial DMSO and DMS assimilation were thought to require their enzymatic reduction to methanethiol. However, reactive oxygen species were recently shown to mediate methane production from DMS and DMSO. Here, we show that this oxidative mechanism can sustain microbial growth without the need for enzymes to directly reduce DMS or oxidize DMSO. In an interplay with iron, both light and heat were effective geochemical drivers of this mechanism that yielded methanesulfonic acid and sulfite, and which mimicked the stepwise oxidation of DMSO by monooxygenases that only enzymatically enhance this oxidation reaction. Furthermore, we demonstrated intracellular DMSO degradation, in which sulfur and the simultaneously released carbon were both utilized by microbes. This study emphasizes that metabolic pathways are not necessarily enzyme-driven, with putatively ancient, non-enzymatic reaction networks taking place at a transition between geochemistry and biochemistry.

title: Comparative slow-pyrolysis screening of nine industrial-crop and cultivated wild-plant feedstocks: biochar yield, carbon recovery and physicochemical variation
summary: Biochar produced by slow pyrolysis is proposed for long-term carbon storage and soil amelioration, but scaling up requires biomass production systems that minimize ecological trade-offs while supplying suitable feedstocks. We characterized
content: Biochar produced by slow pyrolysis is proposed for long-term carbon storage and soil amelioration, but scaling up requires biomass production systems that minimize ecological trade-offs while supplying suitable feedstocks. We characterized biochars produced at 550 °C from nine individually processed feedstock samples of industrial crops ( Miscanthus × giganteus , Cannabis sativa , Crambe abyssinica , Sida hermaphrodita ) and cultivated wild plant species ( Melilotus officinalis , Tanacetum vulgare , Artemisia vulgaris , Dipsacus fullonum ). Biochar yields ranged from 23.8 to 29.0 wt% d.b. and H/C tot molar ratios, calculated from total carbon as a screening proxy, from 0.271 to 0.316. Carbon recovery (40.2–42.5 %) and ash-free biochar yield (20.8–23.3 wt%) spanned narrower ranges than mass yield, whereas carbon content (66.7–84.0 wt%), fixed carbon (53.1–76.4 wt%), ash (7.1–25.8 wt%, all d.b.) and specific surface area (27–195 m 2 g −1 ) varied more widely. Detected trace-element concentrations were generally low relative to selected EU Fertilising Products Regulation and EBC-Agro limits, except that the detection limit for Cd exceeded them; full compliance was not assessed. The ranges of biochar yield and H/C tot overlapped between the two feedstock categories. Because each feedstock was pyrolyzed in a single unreplicated run and sample identity was confounded with site, harvest year and plant fraction, the results are exploratory and do not support inferential comparison between feedstock categories. Three independent replicate runs on four feedstocks showed run-to-run variability in yield of the same magnitude as that among crucibles within a run. Whether diversified biomass production systems can supply feedstocks that yield biochar of consistent quality remains to be tested with defined feedstock mixtures and pilot-scale validation.

title: Microgranulation of biocoke with different binders for effective utilization in metallurgy
summary: Carbon continues to play an essential role in metallurgy as both a reductant and energy carrier. Biocoke as an alternative to fossil carbon provides an opportunity to reduce CO 2 emissions. Defined as CO 2 neutral, biocoke has some applicab
content: Carbon continues to play an essential role in metallurgy as both a reductant and energy carrier. Biocoke as an alternative to fossil carbon provides an opportunity to reduce CO 2 emissions. Defined as CO 2 neutral, biocoke has some applicability challenges in metallurgical processes. To address biocoke´s properties such as high reactivity, porosity and low density, a surface modification technique called microgranulation was conducted. Binders such as bentonite and calcium hydroxide aided in the agglomeration and clogging of the biocoke´s structure resulting reduced reactivity, increased density and reduced porosity. A dosage of 1, 3, 5 wt.% binder selected emanated with reduced modified reactivity index (CRI) for modified biocoke microgranules and improved densities. Untreated biocoke had a CRI of 41.7 % whilst biocoke-5wt.% bentonite microgranules had 20 %, biocoke-5wt.% Ca(OH) 2 with 22.3 % comparable with petroleum coke at 20 %. Furthermore, the modified biocoke microgranules were utilized in a submerged arc furnace (SAF) to effectively investigated their feasibility as a reductant for iron and zinc reduction from calcined electric arc furnace dust (EAFD) pellets. Modified biocoke with 5 wt.% bentonite performed closer to petroleum coke with 96.97 % and 99.33 % iron and zinc recovery respectively. Microgranulation proved to be a successful surface modification technique and a pretreatment method to alter the biocoke´s properties for effective utilization in future metallurgical processes.

title: Energy metrics and neighborhood-level residential retrofit screening: Evidence from England and Wales
summary: Neighborhood-level screening can help identify areas for residential retrofit assessment, but different energy metrics may select different places. This study compares six metrics based on observed gas consumption and Energy Performance Cer
content: Neighborhood-level screening can help identify areas for residential retrofit assessment, but different energy metrics may select different places. This study compares six metrics based on observed gas consumption and Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) data across 33,485 Lower Layer Super Output Areas in England and Wales. We assess overlap between national priority sets, their housing and social characteristics, alignment with official fuel-poverty estimates, and differences across 113 urban units. We also compare EPC-modeled improvement profiles among the selected neighborhoods. At the national top-5% threshold, gas consumption per meter and EPC-modeled energy identify largely different neighborhoods (Jaccard index = 0.029). At the top-20% threshold, the representation ratio for high-deprivation neighborhoods is 0.330 under gas-per-meter screening, compared with 0.960 under floor-area-normalized gas screening. The two gas-based screening rules also select neighborhoods with substantially different residential floor areas. Across cities, greater disagreement between priority sets does not necessarily correspond to larger changes in deprivation representation. Neighborhoods selected only by EPC-modeled energy have a larger mean modeled energy improvement gap than those selected only by gas per meter (164 versus 122 kWh/m 2 /year), while their modeled CO₂ improvement gaps per represented property are nearly identical. These modeled differences do not represent actual retrofit savings. The findings show that energy metrics should be chosen according to the screening objective. Their technical and social consequences should be examined before neighborhood priorities are used to guide building-level retrofit decisions.

title: Anticipatory governance and sustainable innovation as drivers of societal impact: a stakeholder engagement perspective
summary: This research examines the role of anticipatory governance (AG) in forming societal impact (SI) through sustainable innovation (SINN) and stakeholder engagement (SE) in the manufacturing sector. Grounded in stakeholder theory, AG is identif
content: This research examines the role of anticipatory governance (AG) in forming societal impact (SI) through sustainable innovation (SINN) and stakeholder engagement (SE) in the manufacturing sector. Grounded in stakeholder theory, AG is identified as an antecedent capability that affects SE and SINN, leading to SI. Analysis of cross-sectional data from 446 purposively sampled Chinese participants found that AG positively influenced SINN and SE. Moreover, SINN also positively influenced SE and SI, and SE, in turn, partially mediated the relationship between SINN and SI. The findings of this research contribute to the literature by developing a framework for governance, innovation, and SE that leads to societal value creation. The findings of this research also provide implications for firms seeking to enhance societal value via AG and sustainability.

title: Impact of Coatings on the Heat Transfer and Thermal Transmittance of Materials for Space Applications
summary: Spacecraft experience extreme heat changes making it important to study how materials are able to absorb heat and transmit thermal energy. For example, a light color may reflect more thermal radiation while a darker color is more likely to
content: Spacecraft experience extreme heat changes making it important to study how materials are able to absorb heat and transmit thermal energy. For example, a light color may reflect more thermal radiation while a darker color is more likely to absorb it. In this study four materials were studied: aluminum 2024, aluminum 7075, steel 304, and a carbon fiber composite. The materials were tested under a 100-watt heat lamp for four hours, each without a coating and two separate trials with the addition of polyimide Kapton tape and zinc oxide paint. The temperature was recorded every 30 minutes with Type K thermocouples placed on the top side (heat exposed) and back side. The results indicated that the coatings had an effect on the heat transfer, although with slight variation depending on the material used. Zinc oxide paint generally increased the heat transfer of the material while both coatings lowered the heat transfer for the carbon fiber composite. Both coatings lowered the thermal transmittance of the materials with the zinc oxide paint having the greatest effect. These findings suggest that surface coatings have a meaningful effect on the behavior of aerospace materials. Understanding these differences is important in order to select materials for aerospace applications depending on the purpose.

title: Firm awareness and adaptation to climate change: evidence from Spanish firms
source: International Journal of Climate Change Strategies and Management
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine the determinants of climate risk awareness among Spanish firms and explores how firm characteristics and local climate conditions shape the perception of climate-related risks. Understanding these drivers
content: Purpose This study aims to examine the determinants of climate risk awareness among Spanish firms and explores how firm characteristics and local climate conditions shape the perception of climate-related risks. Understanding these drivers is essential for designing effective adaptation policies and supporting firms’ strategic responses to climate change. Design/methodology/approach The analysis combines firm-level survey data from the Spanish Business Strategies Survey with financial information and geo-referenced climate indicators. An ordered probit model with sample selection is estimated to account for potential selection bias and to identify the factors associated with firms’ recognition of climate risks. Findings The results show that repeated heatwave exposure is associated with a normalisation of perceived impacts: firms in provinces with larger decadal increases in heatwave days report less negative impacts on their activity. The coefficients on droughts and cold waves are negative, in line with a salience mechanism, but they do not reach conventional significance levels and are therefore inconclusive. Firm size is the strongest predictor of formal climate risk evaluation, whereas firms in directly exposed sectors are significantly less likely to evaluate; rural location and sectoral positioning shape the perceived impact reported. These findings highlight that awareness gaps reflect differences in organisational capacity and shock type, not merely differences in objective exposure. Research limitations/implications The analysis relies on survey-based measures of climate risk awareness and focuses on Spanish firms. While the empirical approach accounts for firm heterogeneity and selection, future research could use alternative data sets and cross-country evidence to further validate and extend the findings in different institutional and climatic contexts. Practical implications The findings suggest that strengthening firms’ awareness of climate risks is essential for effective adaptation. Policymakers and business support organisations can use these insights to design targeted information, risk assessment and capacity-building initiatives, particularly for smaller and less internationally exposed firms, thereby enhancing corporate preparedness for increasing climate-related disruptions. Social implications Enhancing firms’ awareness of climate risks can support more resilient economies and help reduce the wider social costs of climate-related disruptions, contributing to employment stability and community well-being. Originality/value This paper contributes to the literature by showing that chronic heat exposure is associated with a normalisation of perceived impacts rather than with heightened concern, by establishing that organisational capacity determines whether formal climate risk engagement occurs at all and by showing that selection bias materially affects estimates of awareness determinants when the engagement decision is ignore

title: AVALIAÇÃO TÉCNICO-EXPERIMENTAL DA REMOÇÃO DE COBRE EM CACHAÇA POR ADSORÇÃO COM CASCA DE OVO E CARVÃO ATIVADO
source: Anais do Congresso Brasileiro de Iniciação Científica
summary: Copper contamination in cachaça can compromise beverage quality, consumer safety, and access to more demanding markets. This study evaluated copper removal by adsorption using activated carbon and eggshell particles of 42 and 80 mesh. Equil
content: Copper contamination in cachaça can compromise beverage quality, consumer safety, and access to more demanding markets. This study evaluated copper removal by adsorption using activated carbon and eggshell particles of 42 and 80 mesh. Equilibrium and kinetic data were analyzed using mathematical models of adsorption and mass transfer. The 80-mesh eggshell showed the best overall performance. The equilibrium data were best described by the Freundlich model, whereas the kinetic data followed the pseudo-second-order model. Additional analyses indicated predominantly physical adsorption, with both intraparticle diffusion and external mass transfer contributing to the process, reinforcing the potential of eggshell as an alternative adsorbent for cachaça decontamination.

title: Empire of the Sun: Engineering, Sovereign Finance, and International Governance of Solar Energy Projects from Gigawatts to Terawatts
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Empire of the Sun: Engineering, Sovereign Finance, and International Governance of Solar Energy Projects from Gigawatts to Terawatts By Dr. mohamed kamal arafa elrakhawiIndependent ResearcherDOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24449337 This book establishe
content: Empire of the Sun: Engineering, Sovereign Finance, and International Governance of Solar Energy Projects from Gigawatts to Terawatts By Dr. mohamed kamal arafa elrakhawiIndependent ResearcherDOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24449337 This book establishes the first holistic framework governing the planetary transition from gigawatt to terawatt scale solar energy. Employing a tri lens methodology integrating physics, sovereign finance, and international law, it addresses the triple bottleneck of storage infrastructure, bankability gaps in emerging markets, and inadequate legal frameworks for cross border projects. The work spans twenty one chapters organized across six parts: advanced physics and engineering covering perovskite tandem cells and ultra high voltage direct current grids, sovereign finance economics addressing blended finance and carbon markets, legislative frameworks for land sovereignty and investment arbitration, geopolitical dimensions of critical mineral sovereignty and cyber resilience, future horizons including artificial intelligence and international treaties, and six surgical gaps confronting the terawatt era: legal engineering of critical mineral sovereignty, international liability for regional climate alteration, grid code diplomacy and cyber physical warfare, financial engineering of Article 6 ITMOs as collateral, space based solar power frameworks, and decommissioning blind trusts ensuring circular economy compliance. Five appendices provide model contractual clauses, global regulatory benchmarks, case studies of Benban, NEOM, Xlinks, and Gobi projects, a tri disciplinary lexicon of twenty two terms, and sovereign master agreements including host government agreements and ITMO transfer agreements. This reference serves as a constitutional document for terawatt scale solar governance worldwide.

title: A Review on Various Medicinal Aspects of Moringa oleifera Lam.
source: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
summary: Medicinal plants have been the backbone of traditional healthcare for centuries, and many modern drugs can still be traced back to a plant source. Moringa oleifera Lam. (family Moringaceae), commonly called the drumstick tree or horseradish
content: Medicinal plants have been the backbone of traditional healthcare for centuries, and many modern drugs can still be traced back to a plant source. Moringa oleifera Lam. (family Moringaceae), commonly called the drumstick tree or horseradish tree, is one of the most widely discussed plants in this context. Almost every part of the tree, including the leaves, pods, seeds, flowers, bark and roots, has been used in Ayurveda, Unani and other folk systems for treating a long list of complaints ranging from fever and wounds to diabetes and inflammation. The plant is also unusually rich in nutrients, with high levels of protein, vitamins A and C, calcium, iron and potassium in its leaves and pods. Phytochemical studies have reported glucosinolates, isothiocyanates, flavonoids (quercetin, kaempferol), phenolic acids (chlorogenic acid, gallic acid), alkaloids, tannins, saponins and sterols. The isothiocyanate called moringin and the glucosinolate glucomoringin are considered characteristic of the genus. Experimental work in cell lines and animals has shown antidiabetic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, anticancer, hepatoprotective, cardioprotective, neuroprotective, wound healing, antiulcer, analgesic and immunomodulatory effects. A handful of small human trials point towards benefit in blood glucose control and lactation, although the clinical evidence is still thin. This review brings together the botanical features, traditional uses, nutritional value, phytochemistry, pharmacological activities, safety profile and future prospects of Moringa oleifera, mainly from literature published over the last two decades. The aim is to give a clear picture of what is established, what is only suggested, and where more work is needed

title: When Climate Incentives Matter: CEO Compensation Design and Stock Market Responses to Climate Transition Risk in Europe
summary: As climate transition risk becomes increasingly priced in capital markets, firms face growing pressure to demonstrate their preparedness for the low‐carbon transition. Climate‐linked CEO incentives have emerged as a prominent governance mec
content: As climate transition risk becomes increasingly priced in capital markets, firms face growing pressure to demonstrate their preparedness for the low‐carbon transition. Climate‐linked CEO incentives have emerged as a prominent governance mechanism, yet their market relevance remains unclear. Using a sample of listed European firms from 2018 to 2022, we examine when climate‐linked CEO incentives are associated with stock market responses to climate transition shocks. We find that a greater economic weight of climate‐linked compensation is associated with more favorable market responses. This association varies with incentive design and context. Transition‐oriented KPIs exhibit the largest association, whereas process‐oriented KPIs also show a positive association. Broader environmental KPIs, by contrast, show no significant association, although this result may partly reflect their low prevalence in the sample. Moreover, the association is stronger when transition risk is more economically material, emerges under stronger internal climate governance, and is further strengthened by greater responsible capital ownership. These findings contribute to the literature by showing that the market relevance of climate‐linked executive compensation varies with incentive design, transition risk materiality, and the broader governance environment.

title: Environmental Practices and Household Green Purchasing Behavior among College Students
source: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
summary: The purpose of this study was to determine which domain of environmental practices significantly influenced the household green purchasing behavior of college students at a higher education institution. In this study, a quantitative, non-ex
content: The purpose of this study was to determine which domain of environmental practices significantly influenced the household green purchasing behavior of college students at a higher education institution. In this study, a quantitative, non-experimental research design using descriptive-correlational techniques was used. The Simple Random Sampling was utilized, which involved the two hundred forty-five (245) students who were officially enrolled in the second semester of the 2024-2025 school year. The contextualized questionnaire was used for data collection, and the statistical tools employed for data analysis included the Mean, Standard Deviation, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and Linear Regression. The results showed that the level of environmental practices was high, which implied that it is often manifested and the household green purchasing behavior as high, which implied that it is often manifested by the students as well. Additionally, the study revealed a significant relationship between environmental practices and the green purchasing behavior of college students. Moreover, all the domains of environmental practices, awareness of environmental concepts, awareness of environmental issues, and practices on the need to solve environmental problems significantly influenced the household green purchasing behavior of college students. This only means that environmental practices are integral to the household green purchasing behavior of college students.

title: CAN REGENERATIVE DEVELOPMENT RECONCILE AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTIVITY AND ECOLOGICAL CONSERVATION? A PROBLEMATIZING LITERATURE REVIEW OF SMALLHOLDER AGRICULTURAL SYSTEMS
source: EPRA International Journal of Agriculture and Rural Economic Research
summary: Agriculture must produce sufficient food while maintaining the ecological systems on which production depends. However, efforts to increase agricultural productivity can place pressure on soil health, biodiversity and other ecological funct
content: Agriculture must produce sufficient food while maintaining the ecological systems on which production depends. However, efforts to increase agricultural productivity can place pressure on soil health, biodiversity and other ecological functions, creating a productivity–conservation tension. This tension is particularly important in smallholder farming systems, where agricultural production, household livelihoods and natural resources are closely connected. This review examines whether, and under what conditions, Regenerative Development can help address this tension. The study adopts a problematising literature review approach, guided by Ecological Economics, Social-Ecological Systems theory and Regenerative Development as complementary analytical perspectives. A Scopus search retrieved 1,093 records. Following deduplication, 1,077 unique records remained. After removing non-English records and non-qualifying items, 1,048 records proceeded to title and abstract screening. Of these, 1,020 were retained in the review corpus and examined through abstract-based thematic analysis. Subsequently, 37 publications were shortlisted for detailed examination, and 33 full texts were obtained. The analysis draws particularly on Bisht (2021), which examines smallholder farming systems in Uttarakhand, India, and Schreefel et al. (2022), which provides a contrasting commercial dairy-farm benchmark from the Netherlands. The findings indicate that the productivity–conservation tension is shaped by economic, ecological and institutional conditions, rather than by farm management alone. The Uttarakhand case highlights the importance of common resources, local ecological knowledge, crop diversity and household livelihoods in sustaining smallholder farming systems. The Dutch case shows that improving some soil functions can reduce farm productivity and income. The farm also needed to purchase more animal feed to compensate for lower grassland production. Together, these findings suggest that improvements in ecological conditions do not necessarily secure wider social and economic benefits. Smallholder transitions also depend on reliable market access, institutional support, collective resource management and fair access to resources and decision-making. The review suggests that agricultural success should be judged in three connected ways: protecting the environment; ensuring that smallholder farmers can maintain a decent livelihood; and providing diverse, nutritious food while protecting local control over food and farming. It concludes that Regenerative Development may provide a useful way to understand how agriculture can support both production and environmental protection. However, this depends on addressing the wider economic, social and institutional conditions that affect smallholder farmers. Further research is needed to understand how these relationships operate across different farming systems and social settings.

title: Government Ownership and Market Valuation of Greenhouse Gas Emissions in State-Owned Enterprises: Empirical Evidence from Indonesia
source: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
summary: Climate change has broadened corporate valuation beyond financial performance to include environmental consequences. This study examines the association between greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and firm value in Indonesian state-owned enterpr
content: Climate change has broadened corporate valuation beyond financial performance to include environmental consequences. This study examines the association between greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and firm value in Indonesian state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and assesses whether direct government ownership moderates that association. The sample comprises 14 listed SOEs observed from 2015 to 2024, producing 140 firm-year observations. Panel regressions were estimated using random effects with White cross-sectional robust standard errors. Firm value is proxied by Tobin’s Q, while the explanatory variables comprise Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3, and emission intensity under GRI 305. Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions are not statistically associated with firm value. Emission intensity has a negative coefficient that is marginally significant at the 10% level (β = -3.15E-05; p = 0.0745). The interaction between emission intensity and government ownership is positive and also marginally significant at the 10% level (β = 7.07E-07; p = 0.0787), whereas the remaining interaction terms are insignificant. The evidence therefore provides only tentative support for an intensity-based market response and for a moderating role of government ownership. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because the sample is limited, explanatory power is modest, and the study does not establish causality.

title: Soil Fertility Constraints and Gross Margin Sensitivity in Maize Production: Evidence from Smallholder Production Systems in Hwedza District, Zimbabwe
source: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Applied Science
summary: Smallholder maize production in Zimbabwe remains central to food security and rural livelihoods, yet profitability is constrained by soil fertility limitations and yield variability. This study examined farm-level differences in productivit
content: Smallholder maize production in Zimbabwe remains central to food security and rural livelihoods, yet profitability is constrained by soil fertility limitations and yield variability. This study examined farm-level differences in productivity and profitability in Hwedza and Harare, focusing on soil nutrient status, input use and economic outcomes. Ten representative farm soil samples were analysed for soil fertility status using laboratory soil tests, yield measurements, gross margin calculations, and return per dollar invested. Results revealed moderate to strong acidity of pH 4.3-6.0, critically low phosphorus, deficient potassium and patchy calcium and magnesium levels. Laboratory prescriptions recommended substantial corrective inputs, including 300-2000kg/ha dolomitic lime (calcium magnesium carbonate), basal fertiliser, 100-500kg/ha compound D (N:7, P:14, K:7), and top dressing 300-650kg/ha ammonium nitrate 34.5% N. However, farmers applied significantly lower rates, with 30% complementing with cattle manure, reflecting affordability constraints and limited access to inputs. Yield outcomes ranged from 0.93-3.10t/ha, with 80% of the households producing below the gross margin-based break-even yield threshold of 2.16t/ha and a return per dollar invested break-even yield of 2.23t/ha. Gross margins varied sharply from -USD 250.4/ha to +USD 147.67/ha, while returns per dollar invested ranged from -USD 45 to +USD 0.25. Regression analysis confirmed yield as the dominant determinant of profitability. Local studies corroborate these findings, showing that profitability is strongly yield-dependent and that integrated nutrient management combining organic and inorganic inputs improves outcomes. Regional evidence from South Africa, Tanzania and Uganda similarly highlights the importance of resource access, balanced fertilisation, and cooperative structures in achieving sustainable intensification. This study demonstrates that yield optimisation above 2.16t/ha and 2.23t/ha is critical for profitability in smallholder maize systems of Hwedza. Addressing systematic barriers in soil acidity, high input costs, insufficient lime use, and limited fertilisation strategies requires a dual strategy combining agronomy and enabling policies. Agronomic interventions are implemented through lime application, balanced organic and inorganic fertiliser amendments, complemented by enabling policies such as input subsidies, credit schemes and market stabilisation. By bridging technical and economic dimensions, smallholder farmers can achieve higher yields, secure positive margins and sustain profitable returns, thereby strengthening resilience in sustainable smallholder maize production systems in Hwedza.

title: Sunlight, Hair Oil, and Fatal Engines: Proto-Science Fiction and Anti-Imperial Technology in Turn-of-the-Century Colonial Literature
source: International Journal of Social Sciences & Cultural Studies
summary: Most histories of science fiction trace the genre from Europe to America treating speculative writing from colonies as late or borrowed. This paper studies three texts published between 1871 and 1921 to show that colonized writers helped sh
content: Most histories of science fiction trace the genre from Europe to America treating speculative writing from colonies as late or borrowed. This paper studies three texts published between 1871 and 1921 to show that colonized writers helped shape the speculative imagination from the beginning. The Battle of Dorking (1871) was written by an English-born engineer, George Tomkyns Chesney, who served the empire in India. In his story, technology means weapons, coal, and colonial wealth, and Britain’s great fear is to be conquered and taxed as it conquered and taxed others. Jagadish Chandra Bose’s “Niruddesher Kahini” (1896), revised in 1921 as “Palatak Tufan,” mocks colonial weather science and European scientists. In it, a bottle of Indian-made hair oil stops a cyclone that the experts could neither predict nor explain. Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain’s “Sultana’s Dream” (1905) imagines a nation run by women scientists on solar power, without conquest. We argue that the two Bengali stories present an anti-imperial idea of technology. Their technologies belong to people whom the empire called incapable; they work without war or plunder, and they expose the weakness of colonial science. We also argue that satire gives Bose and Hossain an advantage that Chesney’s fearful warning lacks. All three texts show the ruling power failing at technology, but only the colonized writers turn that failure into a challenge to the right to rule. The paper ends by marking the limits of this challenge and the limits of our own position as readers from a formerly colonized country.

title: Viksit Bharat @ 2047: Navigating Global Economic Headwinds, Technological Disruptions, and the Strategic Imperative for Atmanirbharta
source: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
summary: India’s aspiration to become a developed country by 2047 is unfolding in a world marked by geopolitical rivalry, economic fragmentation, climate stress, technological disruption, and changing patterns of production and employment. This pape
content: India’s aspiration to become a developed country by 2047 is unfolding in a world marked by geopolitical rivalry, economic fragmentation, climate stress, technological disruption, and changing patterns of production and employment. This paper examines how these global developments may shape India’s development trajectory and considers the strategic role of Atmanirbharta, understood not as economic isolation but as the capacity to produce, innovate, adapt, and compete while remaining connected to global markets.
